extraction.extraction_notes:
This is a REVIEW book chapter (InTech, 'Composites and Their Properties', Ch. 19) and is overwhelmingly qualitative. It is on-topic (aluminium matrix syntactic foams = metal matrix with hollow/porous ceramic micro-spheres) but contains almost no tabulated property numbers, so the harvest is small (6 records) and low-confidence.

Records 1-4 are the authors' own SHPB experiments from Table 1 (specimens SHPB #2, #3, #4, #6). Table 1 lists ONLY specimen mass, pre/post length, pre/post average width and striker velocity - no stress, strength, modulus or energy value is tabulated for any of them, so every property field is null and the geometry is preserved in test.specimen_notes. Post-test compressive strain was deliberately NOT computed from the pre/post lengths: the schema's strain_at_failure means strain at failure/peak, whereas the post-test length change is the permanent deformation after fragmentation (specimens #3 and #6 lost 70-83% of their mass), so the two are not the same quantity. Specimen density was likewise not computed, because the cross-sectional shape behind 'Avg. Width' is never stated.

Records 5-6 are SECONDARY, quoted by the authors from Kiser, He and Zok (1999): compressive strength 70 MPa at t/R = 0.12 and 230 MPa at t/R = 0.48. UNIT/DEFINITION CONVERSION: the chapter reports the wall-thickness-to-radius ratio t/R, whereas the schema field particle_wall_thickness_ratio is eta = inner/outer radius. Equation 4 of the chapter, rho_o = f(1 - t/R)^3, establishes that (1 - t/R) is exactly the inner/outer radius ratio, so eta = 1 - 0.12 = 0.88 and eta = 1 - 0.48 = 0.52 were entered. The matrix alloy, particle grade, volume fraction and processing route of the cited Kiser study are not restated in this chapter, so process_route is 'other' and those fields are null.

process_route was set to 'other' for all records: the chapter describes both stir casting and (pressure) infiltration casting as the two routes for metal matrix syntactic foams, but never states which was used for its own SHPB specimens. Similarly particle_type was set to 'ceramic_hollow' because the chapter defines these foams as metal matrices with 'hollow or porous ceramic particles' but does not state which type its own specimens used - this is the single largest uncertainty in records 1-4.

Deliberately NOT extracted:
- Figures 4, 5, 9, 10 and 12 (stress-strain curves for AlF25 / Alf75 / Alf250 and for Al7075-75 / al 6082-75, SHPB curves for Tests 2/3/4, and kinetic energy vs. depth of penetration). No numeric values are stated in the text or a table for these curves; only axis ranges survive OCR, so per the extraction rules nothing was read off the plots.
- All purely relative statements, which carry no absolute value: 'the compressive strength of al7075-t is double that of al 6082-T'; al 7075 gives 'approximately double' the strength of pure aluminium (Balch & Dunand, 2006); yield strength under dynamic loading '~ 45-60% higher' than quasi-static (Dou et al., 2007); 'two had 10%-30% higher plateau stress' (Zhang & Zhao, 2007); 'Dynamic compression testing showed a 10-30% increase in peak strength compared to the quasi-static results' (Balch et al., 2005).
- Non-foam apparatus numbers: SHPB steel bars (1000 mm x 20 mm, E = 207 GPa, wave speed 5890 m/s, Poisson 0.29), the dynamic load factor 1.77, and the gas gun (12 mm steel spheres up to 620 m/s).
- The ANSYS FE model (100 kN applied to a 20 x 20 x 20 mm aluminium matrix syntactic foam cube, SOLID186/SOLID187 and SURF154 elements, multi-linear isotropic hardening). No output property value is reported - only the qualitative findings that Young's modulus increases with relative wall thickness and that peak stress occurs on the inner surface of the particles - so no 'model' record could be created. The 250 MPa nominal stress implied by 100 kN over a 20 x 20 mm face is an applied load, not a measured or predicted material property, and was not recorded.

No test temperature is stated anywhere, so temperature_c is null throughout rather than assumed to be room temperature.

extraction.paper_summary: Qu et al. (Kovove Mater. 61, 2023, 35-48) prepared Al-matrix syntactic foams by gravity infiltration casting of a cast Al-12.5Si-2.5Cu-1.2Mg alloy into packed beds of Al2O3 hollow spheres of three size ranges (0.5-1, 1-2, 2-3 mm), and studied the effect of sphere size and of homogenisation/ageing heat treatment on microstructure, quasi-static compressive properties (10^-3 1/s) and energy absorption. Foam density fell from 1.82 to 1.61 g/cm3 and porosity rose from 35.8 to 42.75 % as sphere size increased, while compressive strength, plateau strength and specific energy absorption all increased as sphere size decreased (as-cast 0.5-1 mm: 88.0 MPa, 66.55 MPa, 20.38 kJ/kg), attributed to the smaller lever torque on small spheres and their larger wall-thickness-to-diameter ratio. Heat treatment (515 C/1 h/AC being best) raised the plateau strength to 87.71 MPa and specific energy absorption to 30.45 kJ/kg, mainly through release of residual compressive stress around the spheres.

extraction.extraction_notes: PRIMARY DATA (7 records): all seven rows of Table 5 (three as-cast hollow-sphere size ranges 0.5-1, 1-2, 2-3 mm, and four heat-treatment conditions all using 0.5-1 mm spheres), joined with the matching density rows of Table 4 and the sphere geometry of Table 6. Note the text mislabels the tables in places: the properties table printed on p. 42 is headed 'Table 5' while the running text refers to it as 'Table 6', and the sphere geometry table is headed 'Table 6'. Unit conversions: densification strain converted from percent to fraction (52.76 % -> 0.5276 etc.); all strengths were already in MPa; densities already in g/cm3. particle_wall_thickness_ratio was converted from the paper's mean wall-thickness-to-radius ratio t/R to the schema's radius ratio eta = inner/outer radius = 1 - t/R, giving 0.903 (0.5-1 mm, t/R = 0.097), 0.905 (1-2 mm, 0.095) and 0.909 (2-3 mm, 0.091). Particle volume fraction is never reported and was left null; the paper's 'porosity' (35.8-42.8 %, from P = 1 - rho_sf/rho_matrix) is total porosity dominated by the hollow-sphere interiors, not unintended matrix voids, so it was recorded in microstructure_notes rather than in matrix_porosity_fraction. Test temperature was not stated (tests run 'in the atmosphere') and was recorded as 25 C; strain rate 10^-3 1/s; specimens 10 x 10 x 15 mm on a WDW3100 machine; no test standard is cited. Process route: gravity infiltration casting (melt at 750 C for 60 min into a packed bed heated to 500 C) has no matching enum value, so process_route = 'other' with the route named in matrix/microstructure notes; cure_or_process_temperature_c = 750 C (infiltration temperature). Schema has no field for specific energy absorption (kJ/kg) or energy absorption efficiency (%), so those Table 5 columns are lost: Es = 20.38, 19.53, 6.61 (as-cast 0.5-1, 1-2, 2-3 mm) and 30.45, 29.48, 27.51, 27.06 kJ/kg (heat treatments); efficiency = 81.23, 80.85, 80.17, 81.24, 89.40, 85.27, 87.39 %. No elastic modulus is reported anywhere. Table 1 (alumina hollow sphere data sheet) is badly garbled by the PDF extraction; the readable values are >99 % Al2O3 with Fe2O3 0.15 +/- 0.05, SiO2 0.2 +/- 0.1, Na2O 0.25 +/- 0.05 %, bulk (packed) density 0.5-1 g/cm3, supplied size 0.2-5 mm, application temperature 1800 C. Because 0.5-1 g/cm3 is a packed bulk density and not the particle true density, particle_true_density_g_cc was left null. SECONDARY DATA (18 records): Table 7 compares this work with published Al-matrix syntactic foams, giving only energy absorption capacity W (MJ/m3) and specific energy absorption Es (kJ/kg) plus synthesis method and matrix alloy; only W maps to the schema. Each row is recorded with data_origin = 'secondary' and the citation in sample_label. Filler type is NOT given in Table 7; where the cited reference title in the paper's own reference list names the filler unambiguously (cenospheres, Al2O3 hollow spheres, expanded perlite, expanded glass, pumice, expanded clay, bimodal ceramic microspheres) that was used, otherwise particle_type = 'other' with the detail in particle_grade, and confidence was set to 0.5-0.6 accordingly. Three Table 7 rows were deliberately excluded: the 'Present work' row (56.33 MJ/m3, 30.45 kJ/kg) because it duplicates the primary 515 C/1 h/AC record; the IFM/AFS row [57] (57.68 MJ/m3) because the cited work is an aluminium foam sandwich, not a syntactic foam; and the stirring-casting TiC-TiB2 reinforced Al row [59] (7.5 MJ/m3) because the cited work is an in-situ reinforced blown Al foam, not a hollow-particle composite.

extraction.paper_summary: This is a computational-mechanics methodology paper: it proposes a finite-element substructure (super-finite-element) technique for modelling metal matrix syntactic foams with reduced degrees of freedom, avoiding both homogenization and CT-based meshing while preserving the disordered interior structure. A two-dimensional 10 x 10 mm aluminium-matrix model containing iron hollow spheres (63% cavity space-filling, taken as the theoretical maximum gas fraction of MMSFs) is used only as a demonstration geometry. The reported results are purely numerical-performance metrics - memory utilization rate versus number of substructures, and running time of the conventional method versus the substructure technique (e.g. 99.95 s versus 31.71 s at 29282 DoF) - plus the optimal reduction ratios that minimize runtime.
extraction.extraction_notes: The paper's subject matter is metal matrix syntactic foams (aluminium matrix, iron hollow spheres), so it is topically adjacent, but it contains NO quantitative Process-Structure-Property data of any kind and therefore yields zero records. Specifically: no matrix or filler material constants are stated (no Young's modulus, Poisson ratio, density, strength, or yield stress for the aluminium, the iron hollow spheres, or the resulting foam); no foam was fabricated, so there is no processing route, no measured density, and no test condition; and no computed stiffness, strength, or displacement magnitudes are tabulated. Every number in the paper describes the numerical algorithm rather than the material: Table 1 gives memory usage rate versus number of substructures (4 -> 2.400 down to 100 -> 0.102, with an evident typo at 49 -> 0.010), Table 2 compares conventional-method and substructure-technique running times in seconds across 162-29282 DoF, and Table 3 lists reduction ratios (2.9 to 12.2) for minimum running time at 2738-502002 DoF. The only material-adjacent figures are geometric modelling assumptions: a 10 x 10 mm 2D model, 0.0125 mm mesh edge length, and a 63% spherical-cavity space-filling quoted from ref [7] (Marur, Materials Letters 2005) as the theoretical maximum gas percentage of MMSFs. That 63% is an assumed modelling parameter, not a measured or reported composition, and no property value is associated with it, so no 'model' record could be created for it either. is_syntactic_foam_paper was therefore set to false with an empty records list, per rule 10 ('no hollow-particle composite data'); note that this flag here means 'no extractable syntactic-foam data', not that the paper is about a different material class - it is a syntactic-foam modelling paper. This paper is a candidate for a separate 'methods/simulation, no data' category if the pipeline ever adds one. Figures 6-12 are plots without tabulated axis values and were not read.

extraction.paper_summary: Buddhacosa et al. manufactured epoxy-matrix syntactic foams from West System 105/206 bisphenol A/F epoxy and West System 410 sodium borosilicate hollow glass microspheres by VARTM, partially replacing the microspheres with end-of-life tyre-derived milled crumb rubber particles (250-425 um) at HGM:rubber weight ratios from 1:0 to 1:5. Increasing rubber content raised foam density from 518 to 635 kg/m3, lowered HGM volume fraction from 64 to 50 vol.%, and kept manufacturing void content below 0.5 vol.%. Thermogravimetric analysis (10 and 30 C/min, N2 and air), TGA-FTIR evolved-gas analysis, SEM/EDS and ATR-FTIR char characterisation, cone calorimetry at 35 and 50 kW/m2 and UL94 horizontal-burn tests showed that rubber increased residual char and total heat release, raised the fire growth rate at 35 kW/m2 but lowered it at 50 kW/m2, and reduced the flame spread rate from 81.3 to 45.0 mm/min so that all rubber-reinforced foams achieved a UL94 HB rating.

extraction.extraction_notes:
On-topic syntactic-foam paper (epoxy matrix + hollow glass microspheres), but it reports NO mechanical properties: no modulus, strength, strain, energy absorption, plateau stress, thermal conductivity, CTE, DMA or moisture uptake are measured for these foams. The measured quantities are physical (density, porosity, void content, phase fractions) plus thermal-degradation (Tmax, residual char), fire-reaction (t_ign, pHRR1/2, THR, heat of combustion, FIGRA) and flame-spread (UL94 elapsed flame time, burning rate, rating) properties, none of which have a field in this schema. Every Properties field is therefore null; the numbers are preserved verbatim in test.specimen_notes and in the per-table evidence items so nothing is lost.
RECORD GRANULARITY: six records are emitted, one per foam composition SYN(1:0) through SYN(1:5). Although the paper reports six test conditions per composition (TGA at 30 C/min in N2, 10 C/min in N2 and 30 C/min in air; cone calorimetry at 35 and 50 kW/m2; UL94), none of those conditions produces a value that maps to a schema property field, so splitting each composition into six records would yield 36 rows that are byte-identical in Processing, Structure and Properties. All six test conditions are instead captured inside each composition's single record.
UNIT CONVERSIONS: measured density kg/m3 -> g/cm3 (e.g. 518 -> 0.518); HGM vol.% and wt.% -> fractions (e.g. 64.1 vol.% -> 0.641); void vol.% -> matrix_porosity_fraction (e.g. 0.2 -> 0.002).
FIELD CHOICES: matrix_porosity_fraction holds the Table 1 'Void' column (unintended VARTM porosity, 0.0-0.3 vol.%), NOT the Table 1 'Porosity' column (47-57 %), which is the total foam porosity including the hollow interiors of the HGM particles; that value is recorded in microstructure_notes to avoid conflating the two. cure_or_process_temperature_c = 60 C, the 8 h post-cure; the 24 h primary cure at ambient 23 C is noted in evidence. particle_true_density_g_cc left null (never stated). particle_wall_thickness_ratio left null (never stated). test.temperature_c left null because the tests are ramped-temperature or radiant-heat-flux exposures with no single test temperature. test_type = 'other' for all records, since none of compression/tension/flexure/shear/impact/dma/fatigue/hydrostatic applies to TGA, cone calorimetry or UL94.
EXCLUDED ROWS: Table 2 also lists the three neat constituents (HGM alone Tmax 228 +/- 3 C, char 63.6 +/- 1.2 %; rubber alone 418 +/- 4 C, 35.9 +/- 0.2 %; epoxy alone 419 +/- 2 C, 8.0 +/- 0.3 %). These are single-phase reference materials, not hollow-particle composites, so no records were created for them. Literature heats of combustion quoted in the discussion (tyre rubber 39-45 MJ/kg, bisphenol resin 31 MJ/kg) are secondary values from refs 36-38 and are not schema properties, so no 'secondary' records were created either. The text states compression strength and modulus of VARTM foam were 'at least 10% higher' than stir-cast foam measured in the authors' laboratories, but gives no absolute numbers, so no modulus or strength value was recorded.
MINOR TEXT INCONSISTENCY: the running text says rubber content increased 'from 10.2 wt.% in SYN(1:1) to 33.5 wt.% in SYN(1:5)'; 10.2 wt.% is the HGM column value and 33.5 wt.% differs slightly from the 33.3 wt.% given in Table 1. Table 1 values were used throughout.

extraction.paper_summary: Al99.5 matrix syntactic foams filled with 64 vol% Al2O3 ceramic hollow spheres (2.24+/-0.13 mm diameter) were produced by liquid-state low-pressure vacuum infiltration, with the aluminium matrix itself reinforced by 0.6 mm nominal size SiC particles at 0, 5, 10, 15, 20, 25 and 30 vol% relative to the matrix volume (0-8.76 vol% of the total volume). Microscopy and EDS showed uniform infiltration with no reaction products, and standardized ISO 13314 compression tests showed that specific compressive strength and specific structural stiffness rose in every reinforced case (up to 49.3 MPa*cm3/g, a 63.2+/-8.1% gain over the unreinforced foam, and +34.5% stiffness at 30 vol% SiC). Specific plateau strength and specific energy absorption only improved at 15 vol% SiC and above, because at 5-10 vol% the SiC particles acted as stress concentrators during plastic collapse; failure was by plastic collapse followed by cleavage-band formation and widening.

extraction.extraction_notes: All seven compositions are fully tabulated in Appendix C (absolute properties) and Appendix D (specific properties), so every record carries measured values. Field mapping: strength_mpa = compressive strength sigma_C (stress at the first peak after the elastic region); plateau_stress_mpa = sigma_PLT (mean stress between 20% and 40% strain); energy_absorption_mj_m3 = W50, the area under the engineering stress-strain curve to 50% strain, reported in J/cm3, which equals MJ/m3 exactly (no numerical conversion needed); modulus_mpa = the ISO 13314 structural stiffness S, i.e. the slope of the initial linear part of the engineering stress-strain curve, which is a structural stiffness rather than a true Young's modulus; specific_strength_mpa_per_g_cc = sigma_C/rho and specific_modulus_mpa_per_g_cc = S/rho from Table D1. measured_density_g_cc was computed as the stated relative density (Table 1) multiplied by the stated Al99.5 matrix density of 2.7 g/cm3; this is consistent to within 0.01 g/cm3 with sigma_C divided by sigma_C/rho for every sample. particle_volume_fraction = 0.64 is the CHS filler content, constant for all samples; the varying SiC content is a matrix reinforcement (a solid, not hollow, particle) and is therefore recorded in additional_fillers, giving both the vol% relative to the matrix and the vol% of the total volume as stated on p. 379. strain_rate_per_s = 0.002 was converted from the stated 3 mm/min crosshead speed on a 25 mm cube (3/60/25 s^-1). Test temperature was not stated and is assumed to be room temperature (25 C). The CHS 'bulk density' of 0.87+/-0.08 g/cm3 is ambiguous (it does not reconcile with the measured foam densities under a simple rule of mixtures, suggesting it is a packed/tap density rather than a single-sphere true density), so particle_true_density_g_cc was left null and the value is recorded in microstructure_notes instead. Standard deviations are given in the paper but the schema has no field for them, so only mean values are stored; the evidence quotes are condensed table rows because the source tables were flattened to one cell per line during PDF text extraction. Process route is recorded as pressure_infiltration: molten metal was driven in by 500 kPa argon after a 10^-4 Pa vacuum was established, i.e. vacuum-assisted pressure infiltration. cure_or_process_temperature_c = 750 C is the infiltration hold temperature (after 1.5 h at 600 C). Stress-drop magnitudes after the first peak (6.3+/-1.3 MPa unreinforced, 22.8+/-5.6 MPa reinforced average) and the fitted linear property-vs-vol% equations have no schema field and were not recorded.

extraction.paper_summary: LSU MSc thesis (P. Wehmer, 2008) on the high-strain-rate compressive behaviour of rubber-modified ('hybrid') syntactic foams: DGEBA epoxy (D.E.R. 332 / D.E.H. 24 / GE-8 diluent) filled with 63 vol% 3M Scotchlite glass microspheres (S22, S32, S38 or K46 - same ~40 um outer diameter, different wall thickness) plus 2 vol% ground waste-tyre crumb rubber of 40 or 75 um. Split Hopkinson Pressure Bar tests at 437-1017 /s show peak stress rising with strain rate (strongly for the denser S38/K46 foams, weakly for S22/S32) and compressive modulus rising ~60% from 450 to 1050 /s. Rubber addition lowers modulus relative to plain 65 vol% syntactic foams at low-to-medium rates; 75 um rubber gives ~20% higher peak stress and more than double the modulus of the 40 um rubber foams.

extraction.extraction_notes: All numeric mechanical values in this thesis come from Table 9 (modulus vs strain rate) plus two peak-stress numbers quoted in the text; every peak-stress vs strain-rate data point is plotted only (Figs. 13, 14, 16, 17) with no numbers printed, so no values were read off the plots. data_origin: the twelve Table 9 rows carrying an SD (S22R40/S32R40/S38R40/K46R40 at 437-1017 /s) are the author's own SHPB measurements = primary. The 'Static' rows and the entire right-hand block of Table 9 (plain S22/S32/S38/K46 foams, 65 vol% microspheres, no rubber, including their 703-1688 /s SHPB values) are comparison data whose caption cites refs [10,20,30], so they are marked secondary with the citation kept in sample_label. The two quasi-static peak stresses (S38R40 58 MPa, S38R75 52 MPa) are likewise quoted from ref. [10]. INCONSISTENCY IN THE SOURCE: Table 2 (p. 23) lists quasi-static moduli of 870, 1025, 1300 and 1400 for S22R40, S32R40, S38R40 and K46R40, while Table 9 (p. 45) gives 870, 1025, 2350 and 2550 for the same samples; the Table 9 values were used because Table 9 is the results table. Table 2's modulus column is also headed 'GPa' although the values are clearly MPa (they match Table 9's MPa column); MPa was assumed. Densities from Table 8 (kg/m3 -> g/cm^3) and void volume fractions (% -> fraction, stored as matrix_porosity_fraction) are attached to every hybrid-foam record; the plain foams of the comparison block have no reported density. Microsphere true density, mean diameter (50th percentile), radius ratio and wall thickness are from Table 7. Strain at peak is not tabulated per sample - the text only says peak stress occurs at 1.5-2.0% compressive strain for all foams - so strain_at_failure is null everywhere. Test temperature was set to 25 C (ambient SHPB testing); it is not stated explicitly. cure_or_process_temperature_c = 100 C is the 3 h post-cure (gelled >=36 h at room temperature first); no degassing or pressure was applied during casting. S32R75 has only density/void data in numeric form, so it is recorded once with test_type 'other'.

extraction.paper_summary: Conference abstract (24th Compatibility Aging Stockpile Stewardship Conference, LANL/KCP, 2002) on replacing obsolete polymeric materials in the LANL stockpile. One of its three sections concerns the high-temperature syntactic foam used as the W76 aft support: carbon microballoons (CMB) in a polyimide binder (Kerimid 601, discontinued because of MDA) replaced by an APO-BMI binder, with thermally activated (TA) CMB and removal of the Thornel carbon mat. Table 1 compares flexural and compressive properties of the 1977 baseline material, stockpile returns, and new 40/60 APO-BMI billets, and concludes that comparable flexural properties are obtained without Thornel mat and without sacrificing compressive properties.

The column headings and all row/column alignment are lost - only a loose stream of numbers survives: strength/modulus-scale values 571, 587, 480, 670, 552+/-48, 897+/-17, 878+/-21, 553+/-22, 735+/-62, 648+/-44; strength-scale values 7.93, 7.51, 5.93+/-0.36, 7.52+/-0.35, 7.51+/-0.40; strain values 0.94, 1.46, 0.53+/-0.04, 0.46+/-0.02, 0.56+/-0.02; plus orphan fragments '76' and '9.'. The surviving row labels are 'Flexural Strength, MPa', 'Modulus, MPa', 'Flexural Strain (%)' and 'Compressive Strength, MPa'. Because two distinct hundreds-of-MPa groups survive but only one modulus label, it cannot be determined which numbers are flexural modulus, which are compressive modulus/strength, and which are flexural strength; those values were therefore left null rather than guessed. Only the strain row is unambiguous by magnitude (the only sub-unity values with a '(%)' label), so strain_at_failure is the only property extracted, converted from percent to fraction. The paper says the table has 8 columns; the five surviving value groups were mapped as columns 1-2 (McIlroy 1977, Kerimid 601, secondary data) and columns 6-8 (as-received CMB, TA CMB, inner support billet, all APO-BMI), based on the text's statement that thermal activation increased the flexural properties (the three +/- columns rise from the first to the second value in every row). Columns 3, 4 and 5 (including the stockpile-return averages) produced no recoverable numbers. Particle loading was left null: the '40/60' and '40/60/5' designations are stated but the paper never says whether the numbers are weight or volume percent, nor which of columns 1/2 is which formulation. Test temperature, standard, density and particle geometry are not reported. All confidences are low; this extraction should be re-done from the original PDF/report if precise values are needed.

extraction.paper_summary: Analytical paper proposing a closed-form model for the thermal conductivity of syntactic foams with spherical microballoons: the hollow microballoon is first replaced by an equivalent homogeneous filler (Benveniste-Miloh), then the composite conductivity is derived with an Eshelby model modified by the Mori-Tanaka mean-field approach. The model system is polypropylene filled with hollow silicate microballoons TK35 (35 um OD, 680 kg/m3) and TK70 (70 um OD, 210 kg/m3) at microballoon volume fractions up to 0.25, with constituent data taken from Liang & Li (Polym. Test. 2006, 2007). Predictions agree well with the literature experiments and lie between the experimental and 3D FEA results; parametric studies show the foam conductivity rises with relative wall thickness and volume fraction, strongly so for high shell/matrix conductivity ratio.

extraction.extraction_notes: The paper reports NO numerical composite (PP + microballoon) property values: predicted, experimental and 3D-FEA conductivities appear only as normalized curves keff/km vs fmb in Fig. 2 (fmb = 0-0.25) and as parametric curves in Fig. 3, so composite records at specific microballoon volume fractions could not be created (reading values off plots is not permitted, and reproducing them by evaluating eq. (22) myself would be generating rather than extracting numbers). The three records above cover every number the paper does state numerically, all from Table 1 and Sec. 3: (1) the unfilled PP matrix conductivity 0.235 W/mK (secondary - Table 1 constituent data cited to Liang & Li, refs 16,17); (2)-(3) the model-computed effective conductivities of the TK35 and TK70 hollow microballoons themselves, 0.06035 and 0.03364 W/mK (data_origin 'model', eq. (6)). For records 2 and 3 the hollow particle is encoded as its own two-phase system: matrix_class = 'other' is the silicate shell (2210 kg/m3, k = 0.17934 W/mK) and particle_volume_fraction is the enclosed gas core volume fraction fc (0.692 / 0.905, stated in the text), NOT a microballoon loading in a foam. particle_wall_thickness_ratio eta = inner/outer radius was obtained from the stated inner and outer diameters (30.963/35 = 0.885; 67.710/70 = 0.967) and is consistent with the stated fc = eta^3. Unit conversions: densities kg/m3 -> g/cm3 (680 -> 0.68, 210 -> 0.21); Table 1 labels the diameters 'mm' but they are micrometres (text: 'the average diameters of the microballoons, TK35 and TK70, are 35 and 70 mm'). Experimental composite conductivity data for these systems must be sourced from the original papers, Liang & Li, Polym. Test. 25 (2006) 527-531 and 26 (2007) 419-424.

extraction.paper_summary: Japanese-language 1994 study (Seikei-Kakou 6(12) 877-882) of low density polyethylene syntactic foams filled with three hollow-particle systems: shirasu balloons (SB, 150 um, bulk sp. gr. 0.25, shell 1.3 um), polyester-coated shirasu balloons (SB-PEs) and glass microballoons (GMB, 80 um, bulk sp. gr. 0.20, shell estimated 1.11 um), at 5-20 vol% in 5% steps, compression moulded at 150 C into 1 mm sheets. Tensile tests at 0, 23 and 50 C showed Young's modulus increases with hollow-particle loading and rises roughly linearly with log strain rate, while the yield stress falls because the particles crush and void near yield; the reinforcing order is PE-SB+PEs > PE-SB > PE-GMB, attributed to shell thickness and surface roughness rather than particle size. Data were fitted with a Bruggeman modulus model (parameter x, Table 3) and a modified Nicolais-Narkis yield relation sigma_c/sigma_m = 1 - B*Vf^(2/3) (Table 4), where B is 1/2-1/3 of the solid-particle value 1.21.

extraction.extraction_notes: IMPORTANT CAVEAT: this is a genuine hollow-particle (syntactic foam) paper, but the OCR'd text contains only the CAPTIONS of Tables 1-4 and Figs. 1-5, not their contents. Every quantitative mechanical result (Young's modulus, yield stress, composite density, the fitted Bruggeman x values and the fitted B parameters) exists only inside those tables and figures, so no property value could be read and all property fields are null. Per the extraction rules no values were estimated off the plots. 12 records are given, one per (filler system x volume fraction) actually fabricated: SB, SB+PEs and GMB at 5, 10, 15 and 20 vol%. Test conditions are recorded for the 23 C / 5 mm/min case used in Figs. 1, 3 and 5; the other conditions (0 C, 50 C; 0.5, 50, 500 mm/min; high-speed 0.7752 and 2.508 m/s) were not duplicated as separate records because they carry no readable values - they are listed in test.specimen_notes. Unfilled PE was also tested as the baseline but is not a hollow-particle composite, so it has no record. Derivations: strain_rate_per_s = 5 mm/min over the stated 40 mm JIS No. 2 gauge length = 2.08e-3 1/s. particle_wall_thickness_ratio (eta = inner/outer radius) is derived from stated numbers, not read directly: for SB the paper states shell 1.3 um on a 75 um mean radius and cavity volume ratio (a/r0)^3 = 0.95, both giving eta = 0.983; for GMB the estimated 1.11 um shell on a 40 um radius gives eta = 0.972. particle_true_density_g_cc is left null because 0.25 and 0.20 g/cm3 are BULK (tapped) specific gravities of the powders, not particle true densities. Composite densities (Table 2) are not in the text; only the statement that 20 vol% filling gives about 15% weight reduction. Shirasu balloons are hollow volcanic aluminosilicate glass; they are typed as ceramic_hollow to keep them distinct from the separately tested glass_microballoon (Tosoh IG102). LDPE has no dedicated matrix_class enum value, so other_thermoplastic is used. The paper's own '30 kgf/cm2 (29.4 MPa)' moulding pressure is internally inconsistent (30 kgf/cm2 = 2.94 MPa) and is not part of the schema, so it was not recorded.

extraction.paper_summary: Majlinger and Orbulov produced hybrid aluminium matrix syntactic foams (ASFs) by inert-gas (Ar, 400 kPa) pressure infiltration of Al99.5 (Al1050) or near-eutectic AlSi12 (Al4047) melt into randomly close-packed beds (~64 vol%) of hollow spheres: large ceramic Globocer (GC, 1450 um, 60 um wall, 0.816 g/cm3), large metallic Globomet (GM, 0.4 g/cm3) and small ceramic E-sphere SLG (130 um, 6 um wall, 0.637 g/cm3), in GM/GC ratios varied in 20 vol% steps and in an SLG-GC bimodal blend. SEM/EDS showed near-complete infiltration (uninfiltrated void content well below 3%) and thin interface layers under 10 um. Quasi-static compression (DIN 50134, 0.01 1/s, H/D = 1.5) gave compressive strengths from 65 MPa (60GM-40GC) up to 180 MPa (AlSi12-SLG); compressive strength and structural stiffness rose with GC content while fracture strain fell, and the small-sphere SLG foams gave the highest strength and fracture strain at the lowest density.

processing.matrix_name: AlSi12 (Al4047) near-eutectic Al-Si casting alloy; measured 12.830 wt% Si, 0.127 wt% Fe, 0.002 wt% Cu, 0.005 wt% Mn, 0.010 wt% Mg, 0.007 wt% Zn, balance Al

extraction.extraction_notes:
Ten records, one per row of Table 1 (all at H/D = 1.5, quasi-static compression at 0.01 1/s). Decimal commas in Table 1 were read as decimal points (e.g. '1,64' -> 1.64; '5,0' -> 5.0%).

Field mapping: sigma_c (compressive strength, first stress peak) -> strength_mpa; S (structural stiffness, initial slope of the stress-strain curve, MPa) -> modulus_mpa - note this is a structural stiffness per DIN 50134, not a true Young's modulus, and the paper shows it varies with the H/D aspect ratio; the 'C (%)' column is the fracture strain eps_c at sigma_c defined in the text, converted from percent to a fraction (e.g. 5.0% -> 0.05).

Energy absorption is NOT filled in. Table 1 gives W at eps=25% with the printed unit 'Jm-3'; the magnitudes (1200-5000) are inconsistent with that unit by several orders of magnitude for foams of 65-180 MPa strength, so the unit is very likely a typo (kJ/m3 or MJ/m3 was probably intended). Rather than guess a conversion, energy_absorption_mj_m3 is left null. The raw tabulated values are: 100GM-0GC 1200; 80GM-20GC 1550; 60GM-40GC 1500; 40GM-60GC 1400; 20GM-80GC 1650; AlSi12-0GM-100GC 1650 (and 2700 at eps=50%); Al99.5-0GM-100GC 2800*; AlSi12-SLG 5000*; Al99.5-SLG 4000*; AlSi12-SLG-GC 2300*, where * denotes values that correspond to eps=50% rather than 25%.

AlSi12-100GM-0GC has no compressive strength or fracture strain ('n.a.' in Table 1) because pure GM-reinforced foams show no pronounced strength peak; those fields are null.

Particle type for hybrid GM/GC blends: the schema allows a single particle type, so the majority sphere fraction was used - metal_hollow for 100GM, 80GM-20GC and 60GM-40GC; ceramic_hollow for 40GM-60GC, 20GM-80GC and 100GC. The actual blend ratio is always stated in sample_label and particle_grade. The SLG-GC record is bimodal ceramic and the SLG:GC ratio is never given numerically in the paper.

particle_wall_thickness_ratio (eta = inner/outer radius) is not reported by the authors; for the pure-GC records it was computed as (725-60)/725 = 0.917 and for the pure-SLG records as (65-6)/65 = 0.908 from the stated diameters and wall thicknesses. It is left null for hybrid blends and for GM (whose wall thickness is only described qualitatively as 'lower' than GC).

particle_volume_fraction = 0.64 for every record: 'The total amount of reinforcement was maintained at high level (~64 vol.%) that corresponds to randomly closed packed structure.'

matrix_porosity_fraction left null: the paper only gives the upper bound 'uninfiltrated void content between the hollow spheres remained well below 3%', not a measured value.

cure_or_process_temperature_c left null: the infiltration temperature is never stated numerically (only the 400 kPa argon pressure and the vacuum-assisted procedure are given). Test temperature set to 25 C from 'The compression tests were performed ... at room temperature'.

Other data not extracted: Fig. 5 gives structural stiffness versus H/D ratio (1, 1.5, 2) and Fig. 4 gives stress-strain curves at H/D = 1, but numerical values for H/D = 1 and 2 are only readable off the plots, so no records were created for those aspect ratios. Hollow-sphere single-particle fracture forces (GC 22.1 +/- 1.18 N, GM 5.1 +/- 0.18 N) and interface layer thicknesses (7/5/5 um for GM/GC/SLG with AlSi12) have no schema field and are recorded in particle_grade / microstructure_notes.

Evidence quotes for Table 1 rows are reconstructed across the line-per-cell layout of the extracted text (the source file lists each table cell on its own line) and preserve the original decimal commas.

extraction.paper_summary: PhD thesis (Choqueuse, Universite de Franche-Comte / Ifremer, 2012) on the mechanical behaviour of glass-microsphere syntactic foams for deep-sea buoyancy and pipeline thermal insulation. Two cast commercial foams filled with 3M S38/S38HS hollow glass microspheres were characterized: GSEP (glass syntactic epoxy, specific gravity 0.720) and GSPU (glass syntactic polyurethane, specific gravity 0.860). Elastic constants were obtained from immersion ultrasonic wave speeds, plus uniaxial compression, a newly developed buoyancy-based instrumented hydrostatic compression test (bulk modulus and crush pressure to 80 MPa and up to 150 C), Iosipescu and modified Arcan shear tests, and DIC. GSEP is stiff and brittle (E = 3340 MPa, compressive strength 98 MPa, K = 2620 MPa, crush pressure 83 MPa) while GSPU is compliant, visco-elasto-plastic and damageable (E = 432 MPa, strength 12 MPa, K = 1930 MPa, crush pressure 32 MPa). Damage was shown to be microsphere collapse, followed in situ by X-ray microtomography under pressure, ex situ by gas-pycnometer filler specific gravity after loading, and by acoustic emission; a self-consistent homogenization model with sphere-removal damage was fitted to a GSPP foam.

Two coupons per pressure level (five unloaded references). No mechanical property is measured in this test; the measured value is carried in processing.particle_true_density_g_cc. extraction.extraction_notes: UNITS: moduli given in GPa converted to MPa (3 GPa -> 3000, 2.62 GPa -> 2620, 1.93 GPa -> 1930, 1.15 GPa -> 1150). Pycnometer pressures converted from bar to MPa (10 bar = 1 MPa). Specific gravities in the appendix table are printed as 'density (kg/m3)' but the values (0.4175 - 0.9935) are g/cm3, consistent with the text ('after a pressure increase up to 80 MPa the specific gravity of the filler is about 1000 kg/m3'). FIELD MAPPING: for hydrostatic tests modulus_mpa holds the bulk modulus K and strength_mpa the crush (collapse) pressure; for shear tests modulus_mpa holds G and strength_mpa the shear stress at break; for the ultrasonic records modulus_mpa holds Young's modulus (G, K and Poisson's ratio are given in test.specimen_notes since the schema has no fields for them). For the 26 pycnometer records the measured quantity is the recovered filler specific gravity after loading, stored in processing.particle_true_density_g_cc with the applied pressure in test.specimen_notes; those records carry no mechanical property. COMPOSITION: the microsphere volume fraction of the two tested foams is never stated. The thesis only says generically that 'typically a volume content of 50-60% is reached for the epoxy material, while volume contents around 25% are obtained for GSPP and GSPU', so particle_volume_fraction is left null. Manufacturers and grades of the commercial foams are withheld under NDA. NOT EXTRACTED (figure-only, no tabulated/quoted numbers): hydrostatic compression of GSEP at 4, 50 and 100 C (Fig. 51 - crush pressure drops with temperature but no values); GSPU hydrostatic load-unload/creep spectrum (Fig. 53); uniaxial compression and DIC stress-strain curves for specimen types 1-4 (Figs. 31, 32, 78-85); modified Arcan loading-rate series on 0.5 mm GSPU (Fig. 75, 0.05-50 mm/min) and the GSEP thickness series (2 and 0.7 mm at 0.0119 /s, Fig. 74); the % of broken spheres vs pressure curve (Fig. 102); acoustic emission hit counts (Figs. 104-105, damage onset stated as ~10 MPa for GSPU); thermal conductivity vs water uptake (Fig. 108). DUPLICATE/CONFLICTING VALUES: Table 18 repeats the test results and is consistent with Tables 7, 9, 15 and 17 except (a) US shear modulus for GSEP is 1115 MPa in Table 18 vs 1.15 GPa in Table 7, and (b) the Iosipescu row of Table 18 (G = 1800 / 175 MPa) comes from the later DIC tests, not from the strain-gauge results of Table 16 (870 / 292 MPa); both sets are recorded as separate test conditions. Table 19 (indirectly calculated K, G and Poisson's ratio assuming isotropy, several values flagged as suspect by the authors, including negative bulk moduli) was not turned into records. Table 1 and Appendix 6.3 give nominal industry/design values for GSEP, GSPU and GSPP and are marked data_origin=secondary; note that Table 1's nominal GSPU density (0.72) differs from the tested GSPU (0.860, Table 3). The GSPP model identification of Sec. 4.3.5 is marked data_origin=model and has no measured property values.

extraction.paper_summary: Japanese-language 1991 study (Journal of Japan Institute of Light Metals 41(1) 44-48) of SBAC, a metal matrix syntactic foam made by pressure-infiltrating molten Al-12%Si casting alloy (AC3A, melted at 973 K) into packed beds of shirasu (volcanic glass) balloons, using two balloon series (A and B) of differing specific gravity in five sieve fractions from 105 to 590 um. SBAC fails in a brittle manner, the crack running through the equatorial planes of the balloons and the most constricted matrix sections; the effective area fractions there are AM = 0.363 - 0.282*VSB and ASG = (1.28 + 0.556*VSB)*h/R, and because the shirasu glass shell (E about 70 GPa) and the Al alloy (E about 72 GPa) have nearly equal Young's moduli, tensile strength is proportional to AM + ASG. Extrapolating to AM + ASG = 1 gives 123 MPa (A-type) and 140 MPa (B-type); the difference is attributed to the lower sphericity of A-type balloons raising the stress concentration factor (alpha about 2.6 vs 2.3), which implies a shirasu glass strength of about 320 MPa versus 196 MPa for the matrix alloy.

processing.matrix_name: Al-12%Si casting aluminium alloy (JIS AC3A), density 2.66 g/cm3, tensile strength 196 MPa
processing.particle_grade: Shirasu balloon (volcanic glass microballoon) from Furue, Kagoshima; type A (one of two series differing in specific gravity, made by varying foaming temperature and time), sieve fraction 105～149 um

structure.microstructure_notes: SB packed bed pressure-infiltrated with the melt; macroscopically homogeneous SBAC with almost no misrun or shrinkage cavity. Fracture is brittle and runs through the equatorial planes of the balloons and the most constricted matrix sections between contacting balloons. Some balloon walls are broken during casting and the melt penetrates inside them (breakage fraction FSB), and the point-count method double-counts those regions so that VSB + VM exceeds 1. Densities calculated by the rule of mixtures are systematically higher than the measured SBAC densities because the air-comparison specific gravity of SB overestimates its true specific gravity. FSB for this composition is stated only as being 10% or below; the value is in Table 1, which is not present in the extracted text.

test.specimen_notes: Instron-type universal testing machine, crosshead speed 8.3 um/s, 10 specimens per condition; flat tensile coupon machined from the plate cut parallel to the casting base (Fig. 1(b),(c)), taken from within 20 mm of the base where the density was uniform. Test temperature is not stated in the paper.

evidence.quote: SBは鹿児島県古江産のシラスで発泡温度と時間を調整し, 比重が異なる2系統のものを粒径が105～149, 149～210, 210～297, 297～420, 420～590μmの5段階にふるい分けて用いた。
一方, 基地金属にはAl-12%Si系鋳造用アルミニウム合金 (AC3A) を用いた。
この金型を所定温度に予熱した後, 973Kで溶解した320gのAl-12%Si合金 (AC3A) 溶湯を注湯する。そして, この溶湯(G)を黒鉛パンチ(H)を介してプレス(I)にて加圧しSB充填層内に圧入後冷却すればSBACができ上がる。
引張試験片は Fig. 1(b)の板材から(c)に示す形状と寸法に加工した。引張試験はインストロン型万能試験機を用い, クロスヘッド速度8.3μm/sで行った。試験本数は10本である。

extraction.extraction_notes: IMPORTANT CAVEAT: this is a genuine hollow-glass-microballoon / aluminium syntactic foam paper, but the OCR'd text contains only the CAPTION of Table 1 ('Specific characteristics of SB and SBAC'), not its contents. Table 1 holds every per-sample number - SB air-comparison specific gravity rho_SB, SEM-measured wall thickness hS, SBAC specific gravity rho_SBAC, SB and matrix volume fractions VSB and VM, breakage fraction FSB, sphericity, and the measured tensile strengths sigma_SBAC - and Figs. 3 and 5 hold the load-displacement and strength-vs-area-fraction data. None of those could be read, so the ten fabricated compositions (2 balloon series x 5 sieve fractions) carry null properties, null volume fraction and null density. Nothing was estimated off the plots. Two extra records are marked data_origin='model': the Fig. 5 extrapolations of tensile strength to AM + ASG = 1 (123 MPa for A-type, 140 MPa for B-type). These are analytical extrapolations, not measured compositions, which is stated in their sample_label; alpha = 2.6 (A) and 2.3 (B) and sigma_SG about 320 MPa are the associated derived values. particle_breakage_fraction is filled only for A 420-590 um SBAC (FSB = 11.3%, the one value stated in running text); all other compositions are described only as '10% or below'. particle_mean_diameter_um is left null because the paper gives sieve ranges (105-149, 149-210, 210-297, 297-420, 420-590 um) and uses a mean radius R taken from Table 1, which is unavailable; the ranges are recorded in particle_grade. cure_or_process_temperature_c = 700 C is the stated melt temperature (973 K); the die preheat was 623-673 K (350-400 C), the melt injection speed 1.0-2.2 cm/s and the maximum hydrostatic pressure 1.4-5.1 MPa (ranges, so not entered as single values). Test temperature is not stated anywhere, so temperature_c is null rather than assumed to be 25 C, and no gauge length is given for the 8.3 um/s crosshead speed so strain_rate_per_s is null. The unreinforced Al-12%Si matrix tensile strength (196 MPa) and the shirasu glass shell strength (about 320 MPa, back-calculated) are constituent properties, not syntactic-foam records, so they appear in matrix_name / notes rather than as records. Note on typing: shirasu balloons are hollow volcanic aluminosilicate glass and this paper explicitly calls them hollow glass microspheres ('volcano glass micro-balloons'), so particle_type = glass_microballoon here.

extraction.paper_summary: 1994 Japanese paper (J. Soc. Mat. Sci., Japan 43(493), 1355-1359) on adiabatic (thermally insulating) load-bearing supports for an FRP marine cryostat carrying superconducting MHD-propulsion coils. Two support concepts were compared at cryogenic temperature: a glass-microballoon / vinyl-ester syntactic foam cylinder (GSF, 25 mm dia x 20 mm long, machined from a cast plate, balloon size 70-177 um) and single/multi-layer hand-lay-up GFRP cylindrical shells (CS1, CS3, CS5). Overall heat transmission, thermal contraction (93-273 K) and axial compressive strength (93-273 K, JIS K6911) were measured, plus LN2 boil-off tests in a calorimeter. The syntactic foam transmitted the most heat because of its large conduction cross-section, contracted more than the fibre-reinforced shells, and all strengths rose as temperature fell; the multi-layer shells were the better adiabatic support.

records.sample_label: GSF - glass microballoon / vinyl ester syntactic foam cylinder

processing.matrix_name: vinyl ester resin (VE), chosen for cryogenic toughness; also tested unfilled as the baseline matrix
processing.particle_grade: glass microballoons, particle size 70-177 um (grade not stated)

structure.microstructure_notes: Balloon diameter range 70-177 um; no mean diameter, filler fraction or composite density is given in the readable text (Table I 'List of specimen' is an image in the source PDF and its contents were not captured). Thermal contraction 93-273 K and the mean linear expansion coefficient over 273-150 K are shown only in Fig. 6: the particulate-filled syntactic foam contracts more than the long-fibre-reinforced shells, whose contraction is close to that of ordinary steel and is essentially unaffected by the number of layers.

test.standard: JIS K6911 (axial compressive strength); heat transmission per JIS A1412 flat-plate direct method; LN2-cooled cryogenic test rig
test.specimen_notes: Cylinder 25 mm diameter x 20 mm long machined from a cast plate, used as the support across a 20 mm vacuum layer. extraction.paper_summary: Japanese-language paper (J. Soc. Mat. Sci. Japan, 53(9), 950-955, 2004) by Todo, Komeda and Arakawa on the effect of CTBN liquid-rubber modification on the fracture properties of glass-microballoon-filled epoxy (GM/EP) used as an aerospace encapsulant. Four materials were cast (neat Epikote 828, rubber-modified 828R, GM-filled 828G and GM-filled rubber-modified 828RG) with 10 wt% surface-treated 3M A16 glass microballoons, cured 16 h at 120 C, and tested in three-point bending and SENB fracture toughness at quasi-static and impact (1 m/s) loading rates. Rubber modification lowered the flexural modulus and strength of the GM-filled epoxy but raised its absorbed fracture energy by 90% (quasi-static) and 46% (impact) and increased GIC by roughly 2-3x; SEM showed GM/matrix interfacial debonding plus shear-band formation around the 1-2 um rubber particles as the toughening mechanisms.

extraction.extraction_notes: IMPORTANT - very little quantitative data is recoverable from this text file. Table I (weight mixing ratio) and Table II (relative density and bending mechanical properties E, S, U) and Fig. 5 (KIC and GIC results) are bitmap images; only their captions survive in the extracted text, so no absolute values of flexural modulus, bending strength, absorbed energy, relative density or fracture toughness are readable. Per the extraction rules those fields are left null rather than estimated from figures. The only quantitative statements in the running text are RELATIVE changes caused by CTBN modification of the GM-filled resin: flexural modulus down 10-30% (larger drop for the GM-filled grades), quasi-static bending strength down 16%, impact bending strength down 4%, quasi-static absorbed fracture energy up 90%, impact absorbed fracture energy up 46%, quasi-static GIC up ~2x and impact GIC up ~3x; 10 wt% GM roughly halves the density relative to neat 828. These are recorded in microstructure_notes / specimen_notes and quoted as evidence but cannot be turned into absolute property values. Fracture toughness (KIC, GIC) has no field in this schema, so the SENB fracture-toughness test conditions are not given separate records; they are described here instead (SENB, quasi-static 1 mm/min on a servo-hydraulic machine and impact 1 m/s on an instrumented drop-weight tower, per ASTM D5045-91a). Records are given only for the two GM-filled (syntactic) materials, 828G and 828RG, at the two three-point-bending loading rates; the unfilled controls 828 and 828R contain no hollow particles and are not recorded. Mean particle size is stated as a 30-70 um range rather than a single value, so particle_mean_diameter_um is left null (full size distribution 15-135 um, wall thickness 1 um, particle true density 0.16 g/cm3, particle crush strength 3.5 MPa). Crosshead/impact speeds are recorded in specimen_notes because specimen dimensions (Fig. 1) are also an image, so strain rate in 1/s cannot be computed. Test temperature is not stated anywhere and is left null.

extraction.paper_summary: Orbulov, Nemeth and Dobranszky (Gepeszet 2008) produce metal matrix syntactic foams (AlSi12Mg or commercially pure Al infiltrated into ~60 vol% hollow ceramic microspheres, 150 um mean diameter, 15 um wall) and unidirectional carbon-fibre aluminium MMCs by argon pressure infiltration, then characterise them by optical microscopy, SEM, XRD, tensile and upsetting tests. The syntactic foam has a density of ~1300 kg/m3, infiltrates almost fully at a ~0.5 MPa threshold pressure, and shows a long compressive plateau followed by densification. Upsetting specimen aspect ratio matters: mean modulus rises from 19.37 to 23.57 to 28.85 MPa for aspect ratios 1, 1.5 and 2, while aspect ratio 2 gives a lower peak stress than 1 and 1.5.

extraction.extraction_notes: 3 records = the single syntactic-foam composition (Al matrix + ~60 vol% hollow ceramic microspheres) tested at 3 upsetting aspect ratios / strain rates, the only quantitative property table in the paper for the foam. SCOPE: the paper also covers carbon-fibre reinforced Al MMCs (density ~2250 kg/m3, XRD phase fractions in Table 1). Those are not hollow-particle composites, so no records were created for them; Table 1 is XRD phase content, not a mechanical property. UNITS: density converted 1300 kg/m3 -> 1.30 g/cm3; volume fraction 60% -> 0.60. CAUTION ON MODULUS: the paper reports the upsetting moduli as 19.37 / 23.57 / 28.85 MPa. These are implausibly low for an aluminium-matrix syntactic foam (GPa would be expected) and are most likely apparent moduli from the raw machine compliance, or a unit slip in the original text. They are transcribed exactly as printed, without correction; downstream users should treat them as suspect. Extractor confidence lowered accordingly. NOT EXTRACTED: peak (compressive) stress and UTS are only shown as curves in Figs. 11-15 with no numeric values, so strength_mpa, plateau_stress_mpa and densification_strain are null. The absorbed specific mechanical energy is given only as an approximate range shared with the fibre MMC ('~30-40 Jg-1'), and in J/g rather than MJ/m3, so energy_absorption_mj_m3 is left null rather than converted from a range. PARTICLE DENSITY: the '~400 kg/m3' quoted for the microspheres is a bulk (tap) density, not a true particle density, so particle_true_density_g_cc is null. DERIVED VALUE: particle_wall_thickness_ratio = 0.8 is computed arithmetically from the stated 150 um mean diameter and 15 um wall thickness ((75-15)/75); the paper does not print eta itself. Matrix: the paper made blocks with both AlSi12Mg and cp-Al but does not say which matrix the upsetting specimens used; matrix_name records both. Test temperature is never stated (tests are ambient in practice), so temperature_c is left null rather than assumed. No infiltration temperature is given numerically.

extraction.paper_summary: This paper presents the design and CST Microwave Studio simulation of a linearly polarized multilayered-cavity radial line slot array (RLSA) antenna at 28 GHz for 5G mobile broadband. The cavity is filled with three layers: RT/duroid 5880 laminate, a low dielectric constant syntactic foam (er = 1.2, 1.0 mm thick), and an air gap, achieving a gain of 18.13 dB, directivity 18.4 dBi, 96% efficiency and 2.34 GHz impedance bandwidth. Syntactic foam appears only as a commercial dielectric filler layer; no composition, processing or mechanical property data for a hollow-particle composite are reported.
extraction.extraction_notes: Off-topic for the Process-Structure-Property schema. The only mention of syntactic foam is as a low-dielectric-constant cavity filling material (relative permittivity er_foam = 1.2, layer height d_foam = 1.0 mm) in the antenna stack-up (Table 1, Sec. 2.2). No matrix, hollow particle type, volume/weight fraction, density, processing route, or mechanical/thermal property data are given, and the foam is not characterized as a composite. All reported quantities are electromagnetic simulation outputs (return loss, gain, directivity, efficiency, bandwidth) that do not map to any schema field. Therefore is_syntactic_foam_paper=false and records=[].

extraction.paper_summary: Japanese-language paper (Sen-i Gakkaishi Vol. 50 No. 7, 1994, Kyo, Kashiwagi, Kato and Kamata) evaluating closed-cell neoprene rubber foam and syntactic foam (10-100 micron hollow glass spheres in epoxy resin, supplied by Showa Highpolymer) as thermal insulation for deep-sea sampling to 6500 m (about 6.7e7 Pa). Density, thermal conductivity after repeated pressurization, and bulk modulus were measured at atmospheric pressure, then used with cell-model theory to compute the heat flow through an insulated container during ascent. Syntactic foams SF-4 to SF-6 (crush strength above 9.8e7 Pa) showed no significant conductivity change after pressurization, whereas SF-1 to SF-3 degraded; syntactic foam is concluded to outperform neoprene foam at depth because it barely deforms under pressure.

Records were therefore built only from values stated in the running text. Six syntactic foams SF-1 to SF-6 are studied; only SF-3, SF-4 and SF-5 have numeric values in the text, so SF-1, SF-2 and SF-6 produced no records. Values that could NOT be converted to schema fields: SF-4 to SF-6 crush strength is given only as a lower bound (>= 9.8e7 Pa, i.e. >= 98 MPa) and the design recommendation is >= 1e8 Pa with glass-balloon density >= about 0.3 g/cm3; SF-2 thermal conductivity rose about 60% and SF-3 about 30% after one 2.0e7 Pa pressurization, and SF-3 about 280% after 6.7e7 Pa, but no absolute baseline conductivities are stated; SF-1 and SF-2 surfaces sank about 10 mm after 6.7e7 Pa so conductivity could not be measured; SF-4 density rise stays below 2% after 1000 cycles at 6.7e7 Pa but no absolute density is given; volumetric strain of the syntactic foam at 6500 m is 0.02 (a service strain, not a failure strain, so not placed in strain_at_failure); SF-4 transmits 54% less heat than NP-6 for a 50 mm initial thickness. Unit conversions: 6.8e7 Pa -> 68 MPa, 3.0e9 Pa -> 3000 MPa. Neoprene rubber foams NP-1 to NP-10 (measured conductivities 0.091 and 0.088 W/(m.K) for NP-3 and NP-4) are closed-cell rubber foams, not hollow-particle composites, so they were deliberately excluded. Test temperature is not stated for the conductivity or bulk modulus measurements (made at atmospheric pressure, presumably room temperature) and was left null. Particle diameter is given only as a 10-100 micron range for syntactic foam in general, so particle_mean_diameter_um was left null.

extraction.paper_summary: An engineering development paper on a 'C'-sandwich radome (three E-glass/epoxy skins with two low-dielectric cores) for underwater antenna systems. Flat and semi-cylindrical configurations were compared by ANSYS finite element analysis under external hydrostatic pressure (flat: 0.83 mm deflection, Tsai-Wu index 1.73, factor of safety 0.57; hemispherical/semi-cylindrical: 0.161 mm deflection, Tsai-Wu index 0.7605, factor of safety 1.4), and the selected semi-cylindrical radome, fabricated by matched-die moulding with hand-laid machined cores and a bolted titanium flange with O-ring and rubber sealant, passed the external pressure test. Syntactic foam is named only as the core material; no properties, composition or test data for the foam itself are reported.
extraction.extraction_notes: Off-topic for this dataset. The paper is a structural/manufacturing development study of an underwater C-sandwich radome, not a study of hollow-particle composites. 'Syntactic foam' appears only as a generic label for the sandwich core material ('the core material is syntactic foam / epoxy'); the paper reports NO matrix or particle identity, no microballoon type/grade/size/wall thickness, no volume or weight fraction, no density, no porosity, and no measured mechanical, thermal or hydrostatic property of the foam. The only quantitative results are structure-level FEA outputs for the whole radome (maximum deflection 0.83 mm flat vs 0.161 mm hemispherical D-type; Tsai-Wu strength index 1.73 vs 0.7605; inferred factors of safety 0.57 vs 1.4, with a 0.5 mm allowable deflection) plus the pressure-test ramp procedure (4 bar/min in four equal stages, 3 min hold per stage, 1 h hold at test pressure, destructive test to 1.5x test pressure held 1 min). The actual test pressure value is not stated (likely withheld for defence reasons). None of these map onto composition x test-condition records for a hollow-particle composite, and the text explicitly says the constituent properties used in the FEA came from tests on standard specimens that are not reported here. Records is therefore empty per rule 6/10.

extraction.paper_summary: PhD dissertation (M. K. John, LSU 2009) on a shape-memory-polymer (SMP, styrene-based Veriflex thermoset, Tg 62 C) syntactic foam made with 40 vol% Q-Cel 6014 glass microballoons, with and without 0.15 vol% multi-walled carbon nanotubes. The foam was characterised by DSC, TEM, flash thermal conductivity and flat-wise uniaxial compression (ASTM C365), and a four-phase/three-phase micromechanics sphere model was used to back out the elastic constants of the equivalent SMP layer and of the foam. The foam was then used as the core of a VARIM-made glass-fabric-skinned sandwich and of an orthogrid-stiffened sandwich, which were thermomechanically programmed, impacted repeatedly at 30 J and 53 J, healed by confined shape recovery and tested in compression-after-impact; healing efficiencies of 100% or more were obtained over 7 impact-healing cycles.

extraction.extraction_notes:
Unit conversions: moduli given in GPa converted to MPa (1.24 GPa -> 1240 MPa; Table 2 foam E = 0.27 GPa -> 270 MPa). Microballoon volume fraction 40% -> 0.40; MWCNT 0.15 vol% recorded in additional_fillers. Radius ratio eta = a/b = 41.69/42.5 = 0.981 (stated inner/outer radii, wall thickness 0.81 um). Compression strain rate 1.73e-3 1/s derived from the stated 1.3 mm/min cross-head rate and the stated 12.5 mm specimen thickness; for the CAI (sandwich) tests the gauge length is not stated so strain rate is left null.

Two distinct foams are reported and are kept separate: (a) smart foam WITH 0.15 vol% MWCNT, cured 75/90/100 C (Ch. 2 and Ch. 4, compressive yield 5.91 MPa regularly cured); (b) smart foam WITHOUT nanotubes, cured 79.4/107.2/121.1 C (Ch. 5, Table 6, compressive yield 20.22 MPa regularly cured). The much higher strength of (b) is consistent with the text ('the one without carbon nanotubes has a considerably higher yield strength and modulus of elasticity').

The modulus 270 MPa attached to foam (a) comes from Table 2, where the text states K0 'is the modulus of the equivalent smart syntactic foam obtained from uniaxial compression tests'; it is therefore treated as a measured foam modulus rather than a purely modelled value, but confidence is lowered accordingly. The other Table 2 rows (equivalent solid glass microballoon E = 1.94 GPa, equivalent SMP layer E = 0.15 GPa) are phase properties from the micromechanics model, not composite properties, so no records were created for them.

Records whose sample_label starts with 'Smart-foam-cored sandwich' or 'Orthogrid-stiffened' are SANDWICH PANELS (syntactic-foam core plus glass-fabric skins, and in Ch. 5 a glass-fibre orthogrid skeleton), not bare foam; this is flagged in every specimen_notes field so they can be filtered out of foam-only analyses. Their compression-after-impact values are structural, not intrinsic foam properties.

Values deliberately NOT extracted: (1) low-velocity-impact results (Tables 3-5 and Figs 24, 35, 37: deflection at peak load, maximum load in kN, initiation/propagation/total energy in J) have no corresponding schema field - energy in J cannot be converted to MJ/m^3 without the deformed volume, which is not given. (2) CAI yield strengths quoted only as percentages of the control (1st impact 83.9%, 7th impact 94.9% of 12.23 MPa) are left null rather than back-calculated. (3) Literature values in the Chapter 1 review are class-level ranges without a stated composition or matrix - 'uniaxial compression strengths up to 100 MPa, hydrostatic compression strengths up to 150 MPa, uniaxial tension strengths up to 25~30 MPa and tensile Young's modulus up to 2500~3000 MPa' (Luxmoore & Owen [7]) and 'Young's modulus increased linearly from 2 to 2.47 GPa' (Kishore et al. [9]) - so no secondary records could be built with a valid matrix_class or filler loading. The only secondary record kept is the manufacturer datasheet for the neat Veriflex SMP matrix. (4) Densities of the foams were never reported; specific heat capacities (1395.6 and 1364.5 J/kg.K) have no schema field and are recorded in specimen_notes. (5) Figures 15, 16, 26, 44, 46 were not read off the plots; only values stated in the text or tables were used.

extraction.paper_summary: Japanese-language JSME conference paper (2003) on the toughening mechanism of glass-microballoon (GM) filled epoxy by liquid CTBN rubber modification. Four materials were cast and cured at 120 C for 16 h from Epikote 828 epoxy + B-002 hardener: neat 828, rubber-modified 828R (CTBN 1300x9), GM-filled 828G (3M A16 surface-treated glass microballoons) and rubber-modified GM-filled 828RG. Three-point bending and SENB fracture-toughness tests (quasi-static 1 mm/min and impact 1 m/s) show that rubber modification lowers flexural strength slightly but roughly doubles the static GIC and triples the impact GIC of the GM-filled foam, and nearly doubles its fracture absorbed energy; SEM attributes the improvement to shear plastic deformation around rubber particles plus GM/epoxy interfacial debonding.

extraction.extraction_notes: Source is a 2-page Japanese JSME annual-meeting extended abstract with heavy OCR corruption; text was read in full. (1) The only tabulated numbers are Table 1: flexural strength sigma = 125, 109, 36.4, 30.6 MPa and fracture absorbed energy U = 38.8, 47.1, 1.99, 3.78 kJ/m^2 for 828, 828R, 828G, 828RG respectively (the table label '838RG' is an OCR error for 828RG). The mapping of the concatenated OCR digit strings to columns is confirmed by the text, which states that rubber modification slightly lowers flexural strength while raising absorbed energy, with the largest relative increase for the GM-filled material. (2) U is reported in kJ/m^2 (energy divided by specimen cross-sectional area, eq. 3), which is dimensionally different from the schema field energy_absorption_mj_m3 (MJ/m^3), so it was NOT written into that field to avoid a unit error; it is preserved here: 828 = 38.8, 828R = 47.1, 828G = 1.99, 828RG = 3.78 kJ/m^2. (3) Fracture toughness GIC (static, 1 mm/min, and impact, 1 m/s) appears only in Fig. 2 as a bar chart with no tabulated values; the text only states that rubber modification raises static GIC of the GM-filled material by about 2x and impact GIC by about 3x, so all GIC values were left out. The schema also has no fracture-toughness field. (4) Relative density appears only in Fig. 1 normalised to 828 = 1 (828G falls to about half); no absolute density in g/cm^3 is given, so measured_density_g_cc is null everywhere. (5) particle_weight_fraction for the filled foams was computed from the parts-by-weight formulations given in Sec. 2.1 (numbers in parentheses are parts per 100 parts of base resin): 828G = 10/(100+10+50) = 0.063; 828RG = 10/(100+10+10+50) = 0.059. These are derived, not stated verbatim. Particle volume fraction is not reported. (6) Neither test temperature nor strain rate is stated for the bending tests, so both are null; loading rate was 10 mm/min. (7) The unfilled 828 and 828R baselines are included as records with particle_weight_fraction = 0.0 (particle_type still set to glass_microballoon since the schema has no 'none' option) to preserve the composition series.

extraction.paper_summary: Hungarian-language conference paper (XXII. Fiatal Muszakiak Tudomanyos Ulesszaka, 2017) on fracture-mechanics testing of ceramic hollow sphere filled aluminium matrix syntactic foams. Al99.5 and AlSi12 matrices were infiltrated around Hollomet GmbH Globocer mixed-oxide ceramic hollow spheres (1450+/-83 um diameter, 58+/-5 um wall) by inert-gas (Ar) pressure-assisted liquid-phase infiltration, and notched specimens (W = 25 mm, B = W/2, S = 4W, a = 12 mm, notch radius 0.25 mm, not pre-fatigued, 4 specimens per matrix) were tested in three-point bending with force vs crack-opening recorded. Mean FQ was 483+/-128 N (Al99.5) and 711+/-126 N (AlSi12), giving KQ = 115+/-30 and 165+/-31 N/mm^3/2; fracture surfaces showed 63/16/21 % intact/broken/pulled-out spheres for Al99.5 versus 27/70/3 % for AlSi12, attributed to the different sphere-matrix bonding.

extraction.extraction_notes: Four-page Hungarian conference paper read in full (including the [TABLE] blocks). (1) The only quantitative mechanical results are fracture-mechanics quantities: mean FQ = 483+/-128 N and KQ = 115+/-30 N/mm^3/2 for Al99.5, FQ = 711+/-126 N and KQ = 165+/-31 N/mm^3/2 for AlSi12 (Table 5). The schema has no fracture-toughness or force field, so no properties field was filled; the values are preserved here. For reference, 115 N/mm^3/2 = 3.64 MPa*m^0.5 and 165 N/mm^3/2 = 5.22 MPa*m^0.5, but no conversion was written into the record since there is no matching field. The authors explicitly caution these KQ values are not yet valid material constants (KIC) - further measurements are needed. (2) No density, no filler volume/weight fraction, no modulus, strength, strain or energy-absorption values are reported anywhere in the paper, so all Properties and Structure numeric fields are null. (3) particle_wall_thickness_ratio was derived from the reported geometry in Table 3: outer radius 1450/2 = 725 um, wall 58 um, so eta = inner/outer = (725-58)/725 = 0.92. This is derived, not stated verbatim. Diameter uncertainty +/-83 um and wall +/-5 um are not representable in the schema. (4) The intact/broken/pulled-out sphere percentages of Table 4 are counts on the post-test fracture surface, not particles broken during processing, so they were recorded in microstructure_notes rather than in structure.particle_breakage_fraction (whose definition is breakage during processing). (5) Figures 4 and 5 show force vs crack-opening curves only; no numeric values can be read from them. (6) Test temperature (room temperature is implied but never stated) and loading rate/strain rate are not given, so both are null. (7) Evidence quotes are transliterated to ASCII from the Hungarian original (accents removed) but are otherwise verbatim; table quotes are reflowed from the pipe-delimited [TABLE] blocks.

extraction.paper_summary: Salleh et al. synthesised vinyl ester / glass microballoon syntactic foams (Potters Q-CEL 5020 borosilicate hollow microspheres, 72 um mean size, 110 kg/m3 bulk density) at 2, 4, 6, 8 and 10 wt% by stir mixing and open-mould casting, and characterised density, porosity/void content, tensile (ASTM D638) and compressive (ASTM D695) behaviour plus SEM fractography. Density falls linearly with microballoon content while both tensile and compressive strength and moduli fall below neat vinyl ester; SCFT-01 (2 wt%) gives the best specific tensile and specific compressive properties. Tensile moduli are reported to be 70-80% higher than compressive moduli, attributed to particle-matrix debonding and to microballoon fracture within the 40-90 MPa range used for the compressive modulus fit.

extraction.extraction_notes: MAJOR LIMITATION: Table 1 - the paper's single data table, which holds the per-specimen density, wall thickness, radius ratio, cavity/matrix porosity, void content and the tensile and compressive strength/modulus values with CoVs - is NOT present in the extracted text. Figures 4, 7, 8 and 13 (density, stress-strain curves, strength/modulus vs wt%, relative modulus) are also images only. Consequently only the four numeric property values quoted in the running text could be captured: neat vinyl ester tensile strength 39 MPa, neat vinyl ester compressive strength 112 MPa, SCFT-01 compressive strength 89 MPa with specific compressive strength 86 MPa/(g/cm3), and SCFT-02 tensile modulus 9.92 GPa (recorded as 9920 MPa). The 9.92 GPa figure is physically implausible for a vinyl ester syntactic foam (neat vinyl ester is typically ~3-3.5 GPa) and the paper's own statement that tensile modulus is 70-80% above compressive modulus is not consistent with any other reported number; it is recorded verbatim as printed with low extractor_confidence and should be treated as suspect. Remaining composition x test cells are kept as records with null properties so the experimental matrix is preserved. Unit conversions: GPa x 1000 -> MPa; wt% and vol% -> fractions (0-1); particle bulk density 110 kg/m3 -> 0.11 g/cm3 (the paper calls this 'bulk density' from the manufacturer data sheet but uses it as the microballoon density throughout, and elsewhere quotes 190 kg/m3 from the missing Table 1). Volume fractions are stated only for SCFT-01 (4 vol%) and SCFT-05 (8 vol%); the rest are left null rather than interpolated. Porosity values in the text are mutually inconsistent (SCFT-01 cavity 57% / matrix 16%, versus 'on average 12% contain both porosities', versus void content 2.7-3.8%, versus 'increased from 33% to 53%'), so no numeric matrix_porosity_fraction was entered; the figures are recorded in microstructure_notes instead. Curing was 24 h at room temperature followed by 4 h post-cure at 60-80 C; no single cure temperature is stated so cure_or_process_temperature_c is left null. Test temperature set to 25 C (ambient; the paper states the pycnometry was done at 25 C but does not state a mechanical test temperature). Strain rates left null: only crosshead speeds are given (1.25 mm/min tension, 2 mm/min compression), and the tensile gauge length is ambiguous (25 mm extensometer on an ASTM D638 dog bone). Comparison data for other vinyl ester syntactic foams (Fig. 14/15, from ref [17] Gupta et al.) are plotted only, with no readable numbers, so no secondary records were created.

extraction.paper_summary: LSU MSc thesis (P. Bhat, 2009) on the thermal characterisation of plain and carbon-nanotube reinforced epoxy / 3M S22 glass-microballoon syntactic foams. Foams were cast with 0, 10, 20 and 50 vol% S22 microballoons and 0, 0.1, 0.2, 0.5 vol% commercial MWCNTs mixed into the resin (NMSF), and compared with a novel nanotube-grown syntactic foam (NGSF) in which 6-20 nm MWCNTs were grown on the microballoon surface by two-stage thermal CVD over an electroless nickel catalyst. Densities and void contents are tabulated for all 16 mixed/plain compositions; laser-flash thermal conductivity increased 86% over plain syntactic foam for NGSF (0.26 vs 0.14 W/m-K near room temperature) while nanotube mixing slightly decreased it (0.13 W/m-K).

extraction.extraction_notes: Only thermal/physical data - this thesis reports no mechanical tests, so modulus/strength fields are null throughout. Sixteen records come from Table 7 (theoretical and actual density, kg/m3 -> g/cm^3, and void content % -> fraction, mapped to matrix_porosity_fraction); nanotube loadings for those rows come from Table 6 and the SF/NMSF nomenclature of Sec. 3.1.3. Four of those rows (SF2200-00, NMSF2200-01/-02/-05) contain no microballoons - they are the neat-resin and MWCNT/epoxy baselines from the same table and are recorded with particle_volume_fraction = 0. Thermal conductivity: the full k vs volume-fraction data set exists only as plots (Figs. 33, 34 and 60, with measurement levels labelled 43, 62 and 91 C; Sec. 4.1 describes the nominal set points as 50, 70 and 100 C), and no numbers are printed on those axes, so no values were read off them. The only conductivities stated numerically anywhere in the text are the three in Sec. 5.6 (plain SF 0.14, NMSF 0.13, NGSF 0.26 W/m-K 'close to room temperature'), which are the last three records; test temperature was set to 43 C, the lowest plotted level. The Sec. 5.6 sentence does not say which NMSF nanotube loading nor which of the four NGSF samples the quoted values belong to, hence the lower confidence and the composition ranges kept in sample_label / additional_fillers. The four NGSF compositions of Table 18 (0.77/2.01/2.77/2.82 vol% CNT = 1.61/4.01/5.19/5.65 wt%, all at 50 vol% GMB) carry no printed property values, so they were not split into separate records; their composition is preserved in the NGSF record. test_type is 'other' for every record: laser-flash conductivity and density determination have no dedicated enum value. S22 properties (true density 220 kg/m3 = 0.22 g/cm^3, radius ratio 0.922, 35 um mean outer diameter, 1.26 um wall) are from Table 2 / Sec. 3.1.1.2 and are cited by the thesis from other sources but describe the particles actually used. cure_or_process_temperature_c = 100 C is the 3 h post-cure (initial cure was 36 h at ambient). Values quoted in the Chapter 2 literature review (e.g. single-MWNT k ~2000-3000 W/m-K, aluminium 235 W/m-K) are for non-syntactic-foam materials and were not recorded.

extraction.paper_summary: Brown, Carroll, Huddleston, Casias and Long (Sandia, J. Mater. Sci.) study damage mechanisms in elastomeric syntactic foams made of a Sylgard 184 PDMS matrix filled with 3M A16/500 borosilicate glass microballoons at 10, 20, 30, 37 and 46.2 vol%. Cyclic uniaxial compression tests to 60% strain (strain rate 0.15 1/s) are combined with analytic composite theory (Nielsen-Landel solid-sphere equivalent plus Christensen composite spheres) and finite-element homogenisation of RVEs containing 60 GMBs, for undamaged, fully debonded and fully crushed GMB states. The composite bulk modulus collapses when even 5% of the GMBs are crushed while being nearly insensitive to debonding, whereas the shear modulus degrades roughly linearly with crushed fraction and is also reduced by debonding; debonding additionally destroys major symmetry of the homogenised stiffness tensor.
