extraction.extraction_notes:
This paper contains only two numeric tables: Table 1 (compositions) and Table 2 (constituent elastic constants). Every composite property in the paper - experimental Young's modulus (Fig. 8), predicted bulk/shear moduli vs GMB volume fraction (Figs 3, 4), vs crushed fraction (Fig. 10), vs radius ratio (Fig. 13), and the RVE-size and spacing studies (Figs 14-16) - is presented only as plots, normalised by the neat-matrix value. Per the extraction rules no values were read off those plots, so the five composition records carry composition, processing and test-condition metadata with null moduli.

Unit/format conversions: GMB volume percentages 10, 20, 30, 37, 46.2 -> fractions 0.10, 0.20, 0.30, 0.37, 0.462; GMB weight percentages 1.8, 3.8, 6.3, 9.1, 11.8 -> 0.018, 0.038, 0.063, 0.091, 0.118. Radius ratio eta = ri/ro = 0.9667 is the nominal value stated for the A16 GMBs. Particle true density is not stated in the paper (only the 3M grade name A16/500) and is therefore left null.

The 0.50 densification_strain on the 20 vol% record is the 'around 50% compressive strain' at which the text says a rapid stiffening of the tangent modulus occurs in Fig. 7a (the 20% GMB composite); it is an approximate value stated in the text, not read off the plot, and confidence is lowered accordingly.

Not extracted, with reasons: (1) Table 2 rows for borosilicate glass (E = 61 GPa, K = 32,790 MPa, mu = 25,630 MPa, nu = 0.19) and for the solid-sphere-equivalent GMB phase (K = 1,673 MPa, mu = 2,478 MPa) are constituent/phase properties, not syntactic-foam composite properties, so no records were created for them. (2) All modelled results are quoted as approximate ratios to the neat matrix rather than absolute values - e.g. 'At a GMB volume fraction of 30%, the bulk modulus is approximately 1.2 times higher and the shear modulus is approximately 3 times higher than the neat matrix', 'with 30% GMB volume fraction, the shear modulus is reduced to approximately 1/2 of the neat matrix while the bulk modulus is less than 1% of the neat matrix value' (fully crushed), and 'with fcrush = 0.05 it is only 12-16% of its undamaged value'. Since bulk and shear moduli have no dedicated schema fields and the multipliers are explicitly approximate, no 'model' records were created; these figures are flagged here instead. (3) The 20% modulus reduction in compression and 40% in tension for debonded GMBs in a glassy matrix (Em = 3.2 GPa) is quoted from Cho et al. [7] and concerns a different, unspecified material, so it was not recorded as a secondary datum. (4) The remark that matrix micro-cracking is absent until global failure near 70% compressive engineering strain comes from the authors' related synchrotron work (Patterson et al. [33]) and is not tied to a specific composition here, so no strain_at_failure was recorded. (5) No densities, strengths, or energy-absorption values are reported anywhere in the paper.

extraction.paper_summary: LSU MSc thesis (K. Chittineni, 2009) on integrated functionally gradient syntactic foams (IFGSFs): four-layer DGEBA epoxy (D.E.R. 332 / GE-8 diluent / D.E.H. 24) foams in which each layer holds 60 vol% 3M Scotchlite glass microballoons of a different wall thickness (S22, S32, S38, K46), the layers being cast one over another and integrated before solidification instead of being adhesively bonded. Five layer sequences (S22-K46-K46-S22, K46-S22-S22-K46, S32-S38-S38-S32, S38-S32-S32-S38 and the unsymmetric K46-S38-S32-S22) were tested in flat-wise and edge-wise quasi-static compression and in drop-weight impact at 1, 2 and 3 m/s. IFGSFs absorb 210-280% more flat-wise energy than plain foam of similar density (stress plateau 8-60% strain vs 10-20%), raise edge-wise yield strength 25-40%, and beat adhesively bonded FGSF by 50% in yield strength and 75% in energy absorption; sequences with the denser layers in the centre absorb the most energy.

evidence.quote: It is evident that the compressive yield strength values have increased from around 32.7 MPa for adhesively bonded FGSF to 49 MPa for IFGSF, an increase of 50%. Additionally, it is found that the overall energy absorption of IFGSF (28.9 MPa-mm/mm) is found to be 75% more than the energy absorption of adhesively bonded FGSFs (16.5 MPa-mm/mm).

extraction.extraction_notes: 28 records = 6 flat-wise compression (Table 6: 5 IFGSF + plain foam), 6 edge-wise compression (Table 7), 15 drop-weight impact (Tables 8-10: 5 configurations x 3 velocities) and 1 secondary record for the adhesively bonded FGSF comparison quoted from Gupta & Ricci [16]. Energy absorption is reported as MPa-mm/mm, i.e. stress x strain, which equals MJ/m^3, so the values were carried into energy_absorption_mj_m3 unchanged. Densities from Table 5 were converted kg/m3 -> g/cm^3, and 'open cell porosity' (the matrix void content from mechanical mixing, as opposed to the closed porosity inside the microballoons) was converted from % to a fraction and stored as matrix_porosity_fraction. Table 5 gives separate specimen densities for the flat-wise and edge-wise coupons, and each is attached to the matching test; no density is tabulated for the impact coupons or for the plain foams, so those are null. IMPACT RECORDS CARRY NO PROPERTY VALUES: the schema has no field for initiation energy (J), propagation energy (J) or maximum contact load (kN), and converting them into MJ/m^3 or a stress would require inventing an effective volume/area, so the measured numbers are preserved verbatim in each record's evidence quote and in test.specimen_notes instead. Plain-foam impact values exist only as bars in Figs. 33-35 and 37-39 and were not read off. Strain rate is null everywhere: the compression tests state only a 1.3 mm/min crosshead speed. Test temperature was set to 25 C (ambient; not stated explicitly). For the four configurations built from two microballoon grades, particle_true_density_g_cc, mean diameter and radius ratio are left null because they differ layer by layer; the per-grade values from Table 1 are recorded in microstructure_notes. particle_volume_fraction = 0.60 is the constant per-layer microballoon loading. cure_or_process_temperature_c = 100 C is the 3 h post-cure (24 h room-temperature cure first). Note that Table 1's wall thicknesses (0.52, 0.88, 1.05, 1.29 um) are about half those quoted for the same 3M grades in other theses from this group; the values are reproduced as printed. The plain-foam comparison samples were fabricated in this study (hence primary) but their microballoon grade is not stated.

extraction.paper_summary: Syntactic foams made by mixing fused borosilicate (hollow glass) microballoons at 2-10 wt.% into a vinyl ester matrix resin were characterised by thermomechanical analysis (TMA) to obtain the coefficient of thermal expansion (CTE) at 30, 50 and 70 oC, alongside neat vinyl ester. CTE fell monotonically with microballoon content, giving a 53-63% reduction relative to the neat resin (30-70% over the whole data set), with the lowest CTE at 10 wt.%. Experimental CTE was compared against a modified Turner model extended to include radius ratio, cavity porosity and matrix porosity, which predicted reductions of 66-36% (radius ratio), 78-44% (cavity porosity) and 80-45% (matrix porosity).

extraction.extraction_notes: On-topic: hollow glass (fused borosilicate) microballoons in a vinyl ester matrix. The paper's ONLY quantitative property is the coefficient of thermal expansion; no density, modulus, strength or TGA numbers are reported (TGA is described in the Methods but no TGA/kinetics results are given in the text). 16 records = Table 1 (5 filler loadings x 3 temperatures, plus the neat vinyl ester baseline which is only reported at 30 oC). UNIT CAVEAT: Table 1 labels CTE as '(um oC-1)', which is dimensionally incomplete for a linear CTE; given Eq. (1) alpha = (1/l)(dl/dT) and the magnitudes (~100 for neat vinyl ester), the values were interpreted as um/(m.oC) = ppm/K and converted to cte_per_k by multiplying by 1e-6. If the authors actually meant un-normalised um/oC these numbers would need rescaling. test_type is 'other' (TMA / dilatometry); test temperature_c is the TMA measurement temperature (30, 50 or 70 oC). Filler content is a WEIGHT fraction (the authors explicitly used wt.% rather than volume fraction in the rule of mixtures); volume fractions are never reported, so particle_volume_fraction is null. process_route 'mechanical_mixing_cast' is inferred from 'prepared by mixing fused borosilicate or glass microballoon with matrix resin' - no processing details, cure schedule or particle grade are given. Particle mean diameter is left null because the paper only gives a 72-75 um range (recorded in microstructure_notes) rather than a single value. Table 2 gives only PERCENTAGE differences of the modified Turner model predictions (radius ratio, cavity porosity, matrix porosity at 30/50/70 oC), not absolute CTE values, so no data_origin='model' records were created - back-calculating them from the neat-resin baseline would be inventing numbers. Model input constants quoted from other works (Eg = 60 GPa, nu_g = 0.21, Em = 22.82 GPa, nu_m = 0.35) are not measurements of these specimens and were not recorded as properties. Note the data is not perfectly monotonic with temperature (e.g. 6 wt.% at 50 oC and 8 wt.% at 70 oC are out of trend); values are transcribed exactly as tabulated.

extraction.paper_summary: Hungarian-language conference paper on an AlSi12 cast-aluminium matrix syntactic foam reinforced with ~60 um diameter nickel-coated hollow glass spheres, produced by inert-gas pressure infiltration. The measured bulk density was 1.58 g/cm3 (about 60% of the AlSi12 matrix, 2.6 g/cm3) and the Brinell hardness 44.8 HBS (about 25% of the 60 HBS matrix). Quasi-static compression of 10 mm diameter cylinders (h/d = 1, 1.5, 2) at 5 mm/min gave a compressive strength of 272.1 +/- 1.2 MPa at 20 C and 250.0 +/- 5 MPa at 100 C; after the peak the samples fracture and then densify, and microscopy showed brittle fracture of the glass spheres and some spheres filled with matrix during infiltration.

extraction.extraction_notes: Paper is written in Hungarian; evidence quotes are the original Hungarian sentences reproduced verbatim (line breaks in the PDF text removed), and the location field gives an English gloss. Only one aggregate compressive strength is reported per temperature ('nearly the same for the different slenderness ratios'), so one record per temperature was created rather than one per h/d ratio; the +/- values (1.2 MPa at 20 C, 5 MPa at 100 C) are scatter and are not stored in the schema. Particle volume fraction / space-filling factor is discussed but no number is given, so it is null. Elastic modulus, strain at failure, plateau stress and energy absorption are only visible in the stress-strain curves (Figs. 1 and 3) and are not stated numerically, so they are left null. Strain rate is not reported; the crosshead speed is 5 mm/min and specimen heights vary with h/d = 1, 1.5, 2 (10 mm diameter), so no single strain rate could be assigned without converting, and it was left null. Brinell hardness 44.8 HBS has no schema field and is recorded in microstructure_notes.

extraction.paper_summary: Collaguazo et al. (Engineering Solid Mechanics 8, 2020, 77-82) fill Nomex honeycomb cores with an epoxy / 3M K1 hollow glass microsphere syntactic foam (0, 20, 30 and 40 vol% microspheres) and close them with 3K carbon fibre face sheets. Three-point bending per ASTM D7264/D7264M-15 (5 specimens per group) and gravity impact tests per ASTM D3763-18 (drop heights 50 and 115 cm) were performed. Adding microspheres cut sandwich weight by 8.6-9.9% and raised specific flexural strength, with an optimum at 30 vol% (71.67 vs 55.1 for the unfilled reference, about 30% higher); specific stiffness fell for all filled groups relative to the microsphere-free material.

extraction.extraction_notes: SCOPE CAVEAT: the specimens are complete sandwich panels (3K carbon-fibre skins + Nomex honeycomb core whose cells are filled with the epoxy/3M K1 glass-microsphere syntactic foam). All reported mechanical values are structural properties of that sandwich, NOT properties of the syntactic foam itself, so they are not directly comparable to bulk syntactic-foam data. UNITS: deformation at break converted from % to fraction (2.00%, 2.17%, 3.31%, 2.14% -> 0.0200, 0.0217, 0.0331, 0.0214). MAIN AMBIGUITY: Table 1 reports an absolute 'Ultimate strength (Mpa)' only for the microsphere-free NOMEX+RESIN group (average 55.1 MPa). For the 20/30/40 vol% groups the column header is 'Ultimate strength f(% Weight Mpa)' and the conclusions call the value 'MPa/kg', i.e. a weight-normalised specific strength with units that cannot be reconciled with the schema's MPa or MPa per g/cm3. Those averages are 64.8846616 (20%), 71.6750053 (30%) and 64.9628796 (40%). They were therefore recorded in specimen_notes and evidence only, with strength_mpa and specific_strength_mpa_per_g_cc left null rather than guessed. Back-calculating an absolute strength from the stated 8.57%/9.86% weight reductions would require assumptions the paper does not state, so it was not done. Individual specimen values (five rows per group, all labelled MI-FLX-18) are given in the evidence quotes; one record per composition uses the group average. Flexural modulus/stiffness is discussed only through Fig. 3 ('specific stiffness vs volumetric fraction') with no numeric values, so modulus_mpa is null everywhere. Composite density was never measured; only the relative weight reductions (8.57% at 20 vol%, 9.86% at 30 and 40 vol%) are given, and they are recorded in microstructure_notes. Impact test records (ASTM D3763-18, 50 x 50 x 6.85 mm, drop heights 50 and 115 cm) carry no schema-mappable property: only striker displacements at h = 115 cm are quoted (1.43 mm at 20%, 1.14 mm at 30%, 2.57 mm at 40%), recorded in specimen_notes. No result is given for the 50 cm drop height or for a 0 vol% impact specimen, so no records were created for those. Test temperature was not stated for the mechanical tests (left null); the 20 C on the resin record is the datasheet's density reference temperature. Microsphere data from Table 3: 3M K1, true density 0.125 g/cm3, D50 = 65 um, compressive/crush strength 1.7 MPa (= 250 psi). Cure: oven 1 h at 154 C, 2.5 C/min ramp; foam vacuum-degassed at about 70 kPa in three cycles before casting.

extraction.paper_summary: Japanese-language short paper (J. Marine Acoust. Soc. Jpn.) measuring the temperature dependence of longitudinal sound velocity of three commercial Trelleborg Applied Technologies syntactic foams (TG-26/3000, TG-28/4000, TG-39/11500, depth ratings 3000/4000/11500 m) and of Fluorinert FC-72, for use as the solid lens and inner liquid of a convex acoustic lens mounted on an AUV bow. Sound velocity was measured with the sing-around method at 500 kHz and 1 MHz between 10 and 30 C; velocity decreases linearly with temperature for every material and increases with foam density (2475-2805 m/s at 500 kHz). From the fitted acoustic impedances the best sea-water / solid-lens / FC-72 combination was TG-28/4000 (total transmittance 0.965 at both frequencies). No mechanical properties (modulus, strength) are reported.

extraction.extraction_notes: Paper is in Japanese (English abstract, tables and figure captions). It is on-topic (three commercial syntactic foams) but it is an acoustics study: the only measured quantities are longitudinal sound velocity, its temperature coefficient, acoustic impedance, refractive index relative to sea water and transmittance - none of which exist in the schema. Consequently every record carries only measured_density_g_cc (converted from kg/m3: 416 -> 0.416, 448 -> 0.448, 639 -> 0.639) and all acoustic numbers are preserved verbatim in microstructure_notes. The densities are the manufacturer nominal values (公称値, Table 1), not measured by the authors; sound velocities are the authors' own measurements, so records are marked primary. One record per material per test frequency (500 kHz, 1 MHz) as required by the one-record-per-test-condition rule; the schema fields are therefore identical within each material pair and differ only in the noted acoustic values. Matrix class, particle type and process route are not stated anywhere in the paper for these proprietary Trelleborg TG-series foams, so all three enums are set to 'other' rather than assuming an epoxy/glass-microballoon system. Test temperature is left null because each row is an average/fit over the 10-30 C sweep (Table 3 values are model estimates at the 18.93 C Suruga Bay annual mean, noted in microstructure_notes). Fluorinert FC-72 (density 1680 kg/m3, velocity ~528 m/s) and sea water are not hollow-particle composites and get no records. No modulus, strength, strain, or thermal property is reported anywhere in the paper.

extraction.paper_summary: Hungarian conference paper (Muszaki Tudomanyos Kozlemenyek 13, 2020) on bimodal A413 cast-aluminium matrix syntactic foams filled with high-purity Al2O3 ceramic hollow spheres of two nominal diameters (d1 = 2.4 mm and d2 = 7.0 mm) mixed in equal volume ratio and infiltrated by low-pressure (300 kPa Ar) infiltration (spheres preheated 500 C / 45 min, melt at 650 C, 5 s infiltration). The foams reached 1.61+/-0.03 g/cm3 against a theoretical 1.4 g/cm3 (A413 matrix is 2.66 g/cm3); CT scans revealed aluminium leaking into some spheres and shrinkage-induced inclusions in the matrix. Quasi-static compression (5 mm/min, evaluated to ISO 13314:2011) gave 120+/-29 MPa compressive strength at 5.39 % strain, a 77+/-18 MPa plateau stress, 43.50+/-16.82 J/cm3 absorbed energy and 64.22 % energy-absorption efficiency, with the matrix separating from the spheres during collapse.

structure.microstructure_notes: Measured density 1.61 +/- 0.03 g/cm3 (the conclusions round it to 1.62 g/cm3) versus 2.66 g/cm3 for the bulk A413 matrix. The theoretical packing fraction of the 1:1 bimodal sphere mixture is 72.8 % from the Brouwers analytical model (against ~64 % for random close packing of a single size), which would give a theoretical foam density of 1.4 g/cm3; the measured density is higher because the sphere diameters are not two discrete values and their circularity carries a 6-8 % average error. CT scans show aluminium that leaked into some hollow spheres (raising density), a few defective spheres, and shrinkage-induced inclusions (unwanted porosity) in the matrix that were not quantified. During compression the foams disintegrated and the matrix-to-sphere bond was lost.

test.specimen_notes: Quasi-static upsetting (compression) test on an Instron 5989 universal electromechanical machine with a 600 kN load cell, crosshead speed 5 mm/min; results evaluated per ISO 13314:2011. Specimen dimensions and number of repeats are not stated (the paper reports mean +/- standard deviation and notes large scatter due to the randomness of the packing).

extraction.extraction_notes: Four-page Hungarian/English conference paper read in full including the [TABLE] blocks. Only one material (one bimodal composition) and one test condition (quasi-static compression) are reported, hence a single record. Mapping and conversions from Table 2 (ISO 13314:2011 notation): sigma_c = 120 +/- 29 MPa (maximum stress / compressive strength) -> strength_mpa; eps_c = 5.39 +/- 0.80 % (strain at maximum stress) -> strain_at_failure = 0.0539; sigma_pl = 77 +/- 18 MPa -> plateau_stress_mpa; eps_ple = 54.31 +/- 0.86 % (plateau end strain, i.e. onset of densification per ISO 13314) -> densification_strain = 0.5431; W = 43.50 +/- 16.82 J/cm3 -> energy_absorption_mj_m3 = 43.5 (1 J/cm3 = 1 MJ/m3). Values not representable in the schema: W_c = 3.23 +/- 1.33 J/cm3 (energy absorbed up to the compressive strength point) and W_e = 64.22 +/- 0.96 % (energy absorption efficiency); the standard deviations of all quantities also have no schema field. No elastic modulus is reported. particle_volume_fraction was left null on purpose: the paper gives only a THEORETICAL packing fraction of 72.8 % from the Brouwers analytical model for a 1:1 bimodal sphere mixture and explicitly states that this calculated value is in error for the real material (measured density 1.61 g/cm3 vs the 1.4 g/cm3 predicted from that packing); no measured filler fraction is given. particle_mean_diameter_um was left null because the filler is bimodal with two nominal diameters (2400 um and 7000 um) mixed 1:1 by volume, so no single mean diameter is stated; the two sizes are recorded in particle_grade. Sphere wall thickness and true density are not given (referred to an earlier paper, ref. [13]). cure_or_process_temperature_c = 650 C is the matrix melt temperature (T_matrix) from Table 1; the other infiltration parameters (sphere preheat 500 C for 45 min, infiltration pressure 300 kPa Ar for 5 s) have no schema field and are recorded here. Test temperature is not stated (room temperature implied) and the strain rate is not given - only a 5 mm/min crosshead speed with no specimen height - so both are null. Figures 2-4 (CT slice, scatter band of the compression curves, failed specimens) contain no readable numerical values. Hungarian evidence quotes are transliterated to ASCII (accents removed) but are otherwise verbatim; the English abstract quote is exactly verbatim.

extraction.paper_summary: A short research note describing production of an aluminium matrix syntactic foam by thixoinfiltration: fly-ash-derived hollow ceramic micro-balloons (5 wt% relative to the aluminium) were placed between two Al-5052 alloy discs and infiltrated at 644 C (78.14% liquid fraction) with a hydraulic press force limited to 5 kN. Optical/SEM microscopy showed homogeneous balloon dispersion and good matrix-balloon anchorage; image binarisation gave ~45% porosity and an approximate density of 1.8 g/cm3, a ~30% density reduction versus the aluminium matrix. Vickers microhardness in the foam region rose to 70-75 HV100 versus 63-67 HV100 for the laminate and 60 HV100 for the thixoformed material.

extraction.extraction_notes: Very short (3-page) note with almost no quantitative mechanical data. Only one material condition is reported, so one record. Reported quantities: 5 wt% balloon loading, 644 C processing temperature, 1.8 g/cm3 density, ~45% porosity, ~30% density reduction. No modulus, strength, strain or energy values are given anywhere (the abstract mentions standardized compression tests but no results are shown), so all Properties fields are null. Vickers hardness (63-75 HV100, Table 2) has no schema field and is recorded in specimen_notes only. The 45% 'average porosity' from image binarisation is the total hollow/pore area including the balloon interiors, not unintended matrix porosity, so matrix_porosity_fraction was left null and the value placed in microstructure_notes. Balloon true density is given only as a range (0.6-0.8 g/cm3) so it was left null. Balloon size is reported as two orthogonal dimensions (266.185 um length, 197.745 um width) rather than a mean diameter, and the radius ratio eta is not stated (only a 2.5 um wall thickness), so both fields were left null rather than derived. Test temperature assumed room temperature (25 C) for the hardness test.

extraction.paper_summary: Spanish-language PhD thesis (UPM, 2021) on aluminium syntactic foams (ASF / metal matrix syntactic foams) made by mechanically-assisted gravity melt infiltration (DIM) of an AA6063 (Al-Mg-Si) matrix into beds of porous nodules. Two series were produced: C-ASF, reinforced with ~11.5 mm expanded-clay (Arlita/LECA) nodules infiltrated at 700 C, and T-ASF, reinforced with in-house 8-9 mm foamed commercially-pure aluminium nodules (TPM, foamed with marble/CaCO3) infiltrated at 750 C. Samples were annealed (AA6063-O) and compressed quasi-statically (1e-3 1/s, 20 C) per ISO 13314:2011; T-ASF gave higher quasi-elastic gradient (mean 525 MPa vs 325 MPa) and slightly higher yield, while C-ASF absorbed ~20-24% more energy because of its longer plateau, and the Goga viscoelastic model was validated for both series.

extraction.extraction_notes: 1) Text is Spanish; property names mapped as follows: Gqs (gradiente cuasi-elastico, ISO 13314 quasi-elastic gradient) -> modulus_mpa; Sry (tension relativa a compresion, 0.2% plastic strain) -> strength_mpa; Spl (tension plateau) -> plateau_stress_mpa; Eple (deformacion final del regimen plateau) -> densification_strain; W(Eple) -> energy_absorption_mj_m3. 2) Tables use the comma as decimal separator (e.g. '324,570' = 324.570 MPa); values transcribed with a decimal point. 3) measured_density_g_cc is NOT tabulated per sample. It was computed as (relative density from Tabla 5-11/5-12) x 2.70 g/cm3, the AA6063 density stated in Tabla 4-4. The results fall inside the ranges the paper states in text (T-ASF 1440-1623 kg/m3, C-ASF 1560-1670 kg/m3), so the derivation is consistent, but these are derived not directly quoted. Relative density is also recorded verbatim in microstructure_notes. 4) Total porosity (Tabla 5-11/5-12) is reported in microstructure_notes rather than matrix_porosity_fraction, because that column is the TOTAL foam porosity, not the unintended matrix/residual porosity. The paper gives residual/matrix porosity only as series averages (~10% for T-ASF, ~3% for C-ASF, Conclusion 4), so it was not attributed to individual samples and matrix_porosity_fraction is left null. 5) particle_true_density_g_cc is given only for the TPM nodules as a stated mean (820 kg/m3 = 0.820 g/cm3); for the Arlita nodules only ranges (700-870 kg/m3) are given, so it is left null. 6) Samples C-ASF01, C-ASF06, T-ASF05 and T-ASF07 were physically characterised but not compression tested; they are recorded with test_type 'other' and null mechanical properties. 7) Standalone compression tests on the nodules themselves (Tablas 5-2, 5-7 to 5-10, series ARL-NT/TT and TPM-NTV/TTV/NTH/TTH) are constituent-particle data, not hollow-particle-composite data, and are therefore not extracted as records. 8) Stress-strain curves (Figuras 5-74, 5-75) were not read off; only tabulated values were used. 9) Conductivity results (%IACS) have no schema field and were omitted. 10) All samples were annealed at 415 C / 180 min (AA6063-O) before testing.

extraction.paper_summary: Kitahara, Akiyama and Ueno (Journal of Japan Institute of Light Metals, 40(12), 1990, in Japanese) study a metal-matrix syntactic foam, 'SBAC', made of Shirasu Balloons (SB - volcanic hollow glass microballoons, specific gravity 0.563, 149-210 um) in an Al-12%Si casting alloy (AC3A). The SB volume fraction VSB was varied from 0 to 60 vol% by packing SB together with 149-490 um Al-12%Si alloy powder into a die and pressure-infiltrating molten Al-12%Si into the interstices. Tensile strength, compressive strength, shear modulus, internal friction coefficient and electrical conductivity were measured against VSB: shear modulus fell exponentially and monotonically and followed a logarithmic mixture rule (Kerner and Takano models did not fit), while tensile strength, compressive strength and conductivity fell exponentially with a sharp downward knee near 50 vol% and internal friction rose linearly with a sharp upward knee at the same point, attributed to a rapid increase in SB-SB contact points above the loosest cubic packing fraction (52.4 vol%).

extraction.extraction_notes:
MAJOR CAVEAT: this 1990 Japanese-language paper reports the whole VSB dependence graphically only. Tensile strength and compressive strength vs VSB (Fig. 1 and the log-log Fig. 5), shear modulus and internal friction vs VSB (Fig. 2) and specific conductivity vs VSB (Fig. 3) carry no numeric values in the text and there is no data table for the composites. The only property values stated numerically anywhere in the text are those of the SB-free matrix baseline (VSB = 0). Therefore NO record could be created for any actual SB-containing composition, even though the study covers VSB = 0-60 vol%; reading values off the figures is not permitted. The three records here are all the VSB = 0 matrix baseline, one per test type (tension, compression, torsion/shear).

The paper is definitely on-topic: SBAC is an Al-12%Si matrix syntactic foam filled with hollow volcanic glass microballoons (Shirasu Balloons), made by pressure infiltration of molten alloy into a die pre-packed with SB plus 149-490 um Al-12%Si alloy powder.

DERIVED VALUES (flagged, not stated verbatim in the paper):
- particle_mean_diameter_um = 179.6 um, from the stated mean particle RADIUS R = 89.8 um (x2). Size range given as 149-210 um diameter.
- particle_wall_thickness_ratio = 0.9422, computed as eta = (R - h)/R from the stated R = 89.8 um and measured wall thickness h = 5.19 um.
- strain_rate_per_s: the paper gives only the crosshead speed (8.33 um/s, identical for tension and compression). Nominal rates were computed as speed / specimen length: 8.33e-3 mm/s / 15 mm parallel length = 5.55e-4 1/s (tension) and / 20 mm height = 4.17e-4 1/s (compression). Both are quasi-static.

UNIT / TYPO NOTES: 'G=27.4Pa' in the results paragraph is a typo for 27.4 GPa (confirmed by the later sentence using 'the measured value 27.4 GPa'); recorded as 27400 MPa. The internal friction coefficient Q^-1 = 0.0040 is mapped to loss_tangent (Q^-1 = tan delta). SB specific gravity 0.563 is used as particle_true_density_g_cc.

NOT REPRESENTABLE IN THE SCHEMA: electrical conductivity of the matrix, C = 8.40 MS/m (and the whole conductivity-vs-VSB curve), has no schema field and is not recorded. Compressive strength for VSB <= 10 vol% is a 0.2% proof stress, not a peak stress (footnote *1).

MODEL / CONSTITUENT VALUES NOT MADE INTO RECORDS (they are properties of the balloons or the glass, not of a composite specimen): apparent bulk modulus of SB KSB = 3.45 GPa; apparent shear modulus of SB GSB estimated as 2.38 GPa (elastic relation), 3.15 GPa (Takano model), 3.44 GPa (log mixture-rule least-squares fit, eq. 4) - note the conclusions section instead quotes GSB = 2.63 GPa and Gm = 27.4 GPa, which is inconsistent with the 27.2 / 3.44 GPa pair given in eq. (4) in the body; Shirasu glass wall properties calculated from oxide composition, ESG = 69.9 GPa, GSG = 28.6 GPa, nu_SG = 0.22. Kerner's and Takano's mixture rules were both found not to fit; the empirical logarithmic mixture rule log G = (1-VSB) log Gm + VSB log GSB fitted well.

extraction.paper_summary: Cinar (Eur. J. Eng. App. Sci. 2022) develops a syntactic foam from MGS R285/H285 epoxy filled with 56 wt% expanded (porous) recycled-glass granules of 1-2 mm, and uses it as a filler core inside 6060-T6 aluminum circular tubes (20 mm OD, 1 mm wall, 25 mm high). Quasi-static axial compression tests compare empty base tubes (BT), bare syntactic foam (SF) and foam-filled tubes (FFT). Foam filling changed the tube collapse mode from diamond to ring/concertina, and the foam-filled tube absorbed more energy than the sum of the separate tube and foam, indicating a tube-foam interaction effect; the addition of the foam raised specific absorbed energy by 42% and absorbed energy by 188%.

MAJOR CAVEAT: this 5-page short paper reports essentially all of its measured mechanical results in figures only. Load-displacement curves (Fig. 2), the interaction-effect area (Fig. 4) and the specific absorbed energy / absorbed energy bar charts (Fig. 6) carry no numeric values in the text, and there is no results table. Consequently no modulus, strength, plateau stress, densification strain or energy absorption value could be extracted for the syntactic foam, the base tube or the foam-filled tube - only the relative improvements '42% higher specific absorbed energy' and '188% higher absorbed energy' for the foam-filled tube versus the empty tube are stated, which cannot be converted to absolute schema units. Those fields are left null per the no-invented-numbers rule.

PARTICLE TYPE: the filler is expanded (foamed) recycled glass granules, i.e. porous rather than single-cavity hollow microballoons, and is coarse (1-2 mm) compared with typical microballoons, so particle_type is set to 'other' rather than glass_microballoon. The paper nevertheless calls the material a syntactic foam throughout, so is_syntactic_foam_paper=true.

DENSITY AMBIGUITY: Table 1 lists the expanded glass 'Density (kg/m3) 230' without stating whether this is the poured bulk density of the granules or the true particle density; it is recorded as particle_true_density_g_cc = 0.23 (230 kg/m3 / 1000) with this caveat.

COMPOSITION: only a mass (weight) fraction of 56% expanded glass is reported; no volume fraction is given and no conversion was attempted, so particle_volume_fraction is null. Particle size is given only as a 1-2 mm range with no mean, so particle_mean_diameter_um is null and the range is recorded in microstructure_notes.

NOT EXTRACTED AS RECORDS: the 6060-T6 aluminum tube properties in Table 2 (yield 195 MPa, tensile 230 MPa, E 69 GPa, elongation 12%) describe the metal tube, not a hollow-particle composite, and the base tube (BT) and foam-filled tube (FFT) configurations are structural assemblies rather than foam compositions; none of these produced usable material-property numbers anyway. The neat cured resin record is supplier datasheet data (Ref. [26]) included as a filler-free matrix baseline and marked secondary; particle_type there is 'other' at zero fraction only because the schema requires a particle type.

UNIT CONVERSIONS: elastic modulus 3.2 GPa -> 3200 MPa; expanded glass density 230 kg/m3 -> 0.23 g/cm3.

extraction.paper_summary: Metal matrix syntactic foams were produced by low-pressure (500 kPa argon) infiltration of molten A356 aluminium (7Si-0.3Mg) at 840 C into a mixture of Glober Al2O3 ceramic hollow spheres (2.29 +- 0.16 mm) and 20 wt% ceramic reinforcing grains, then T6 heat treated. Four reinforcements were compared with a non-reinforced reference: FS 18, FS 40 and FS 46 Al2O3 grains and FS 46 SiC grains. Quasi-static compression tests to ISO 13314:2011 show the matrix reinforcement always raises compressive strength (by more than 17 % on average, from 108.2 MPa to 116.4-133.8 MPa) but generally lowers the energy absorbed up to 50 % strain; FS 18 Al2O3 performed best.

extraction.paper_summary: Singh, Kumar, Sachan and Sharma (IJERMCE 9(7), 2022) present a short student-level study titled 'Synthesis and Characterization of Syntactic foam'. After a general review of syntactic-foam types (two- vs three-phase, MMC/PMC/CMC), the actual experiment takes a commercially porous polypropylene foam as the matrix, submerges it in a semi-fluid Plaster of Paris paste so the existing pores fill up, dries it and bakes it for 1.5 h at 220 C, then compression-tests it on a UTM against a red brick reference. The reported outcome is a 35.35% density reduction (1239.90 kg/m3 vs 1922 kg/m3 for red brick) and a ~63% drop in breaking stress; the authors recommend the material only where strength is not required.
extraction.extraction_notes:
OFF-TOPIC / EXCLUDED under rule 6: this is not a hollow-particle composite. No microballoons, cenospheres or hollow spheres of any kind are added to a matrix. The authors instead take an already-cellular polypropylene foam ('microballoons are already present in it') and infiltrate its open pores with a Plaster of Paris paste - i.e. a filled cellular/open-cell foam, which is the inverse of syntactic-foam architecture (in a syntactic foam the hollow phase is a discrete particle dispersed in a dense matrix; here the solid phase is poured into the cells and the hollow phase ceases to be hollow). is_syntactic_foam_paper is therefore set false and records is empty. Only the paper's title and framing are about syntactic foams; the hollow-particle systems it cites (epoxy/hollow glass microspheres, fly-ash cenosphere/polyurethane) appear in the two-line literature review with no numerical data at all.

For a human reviewer who may wish to override this call, the numbers that exist are recorded here rather than as records, and they are unusable as they stand. Table (b) 'Syntactic foam': specimen 45.00 mm wide x 40 mm thick, cross-section 2700.0 mm2 (45 x 40 = 1800, not 2700 - the geometry is already inconsistent), peak load 5.130, compressive strength 0.194 kg/mm2, elongation at break 6.99 mm, breaking load 39.49 kN, breaking stress 0.523 kN/mm2. The last three of those are byte-identical to the red-brick row in Table (a) (6.99 / 39.49 / 0.523), so Table (b) is a copy-paste of the reference specimen's results. Table (c) then contradicts Table (b), giving the foam a breaking stress of 0.192 kg/mm2 and a yield stress of 0.165 kN/mm2 - and the two tables also swap the units between kg/mm2 and kN/mm2 for the same quantity (0.165 kN/mm2 would be 165 MPa yield for a plaster-filled polypropylene foam, which is physically impossible; red brick at 0.610 kN/mm2 = 610 MPa likewise). Load units for 'peak load' are never given. Because every strength value in the paper is either duplicated from another specimen or carries a unit that is off by orders of magnitude, no strength could be converted to MPa without inventing an interpretation, and none was.

The one internally consistent, unit-labelled figure is the measured density of the tested material, 1239.90 kg/m3 = 1.2399 g/cm3 (Table (c)); it is noted here only, since the specimen it belongs to is not a hollow-particle composite. No modulus, strain rate, test standard or test temperature is reported anywhere in the paper.

extraction.paper_summary: Doctoral thesis (Afolabi, Durban University of Technology) on epoxy syntactic foam composites (SFC) made by open resin casting/stir mixing with degassing of DGEBA epoxy (LR 20 / LH281) filled with T60 hollow glass microspheres (true density 0.6 g/cc, radius ratio 0.9141) at 5-25 vol%, used both as heterogeneous (as-received, whole size distribution) filler and as four sieved homogeneous size classes AA 20-24, BB 25-44, CC 45-49 and DD 50-60 um. Density, tensile, flexural, impact, hardness, water absorption, buoyancy, TGA and DMA properties were measured; tensile modulus peaked at 4.63 GPa (EPT60-15) and flexural strength at 118 MPa (EPT60-25), both far above the neat epoxy, while the homogeneous size-classified foams generally showed lower moduli than the heterogeneous ones. The SFC was then used as the core of hybrid sandwich panels with kenaf and/or glass fibre face sheets (KK, GG, GK, KG), whose density, tensile, flexural, edgewise-compression, shear, water-absorption, buoyancy and acoustic properties were measured and compared with series/parallel/Hirsch models.

extraction.extraction_notes: Units: all moduli converted GPa -> MPa; tan delta values in Table 9.7 are tabulated as 'x10^3' and were divided by 1000; volume fractions converted from % to fractions; sandwich porosity (void) % converted to a fraction in matrix_porosity_fraction. particle_volume_fraction for the sieved homogeneous foams uses the nominal 5-25 vol% loading; particle_true_density_g_cc uses the size-class powder density rho_d of Table 4.2 (OO 0.600, AA 0.7548, BB 0.7286, CC 0.7083, DD 0.5529 g/cc) and particle_mean_diameter_um the measured mean diameter d of the same table (OO 39.26, AA 29.62, BB 30.86, CC 29.40, DD 55.04 um); Table 3.1 quotes the manufacturer's nominal T60 true density of 0.6 g/cc for all sizes. SFC bulk densities per composition are only shown graphically (Figs. 5.2-5.4), so measured_density_g_cc is left null for all SFC records even though the tables report specific (density-normalised) properties; only the sandwich panels have tabulated densities (Table 8.1). Table 7.2 restates the present-work flexural moduli as 2359/3485/3728/3931/4292/5752 MPa, which differ slightly from the 2.4/3.5/3.7/3.9/4.3/4.8 GPa of Table 7.1; the Table 7.1 values (consistent with the narrative text) were used. Table 7.2 also lists neat-epoxy flexural strength as 53.3 MPa vs 53.5 MPa in Table 7.1; 53.5 was used. Charpy impact results (neat epoxy 84.57 kJ/m2, EPT60-5 113.12 kJ/m2, remaining compositions given only as percentage increases that are inconsistent with the quoted peak value) are reported per unit area, which cannot be converted to the schema's MJ/m3 energy_absorption field, so no impact records were created. TGA decomposition temperatures (Tables 9.1-9.2), Tg/Tmax (Table 9.4), loss modulus E'' (Tables 9.5-9.6), Barcol hardness (Tables 10.1-10.2), buoyancy force (Tables 10.7-10.8) and acoustic sound level/pressure (Tables 10.9-10.10) have no corresponding schema field and were omitted. The HGM volume fraction of the syntactic-foam core used in the sandwich panels is never stated; the modelling tables (8.7/8.8) use SFC modulus 4.57 GPa and strength 66.73 MPa, i.e. the EPT60-20 heterogeneous foam, so core particle_volume_fraction is left null and noted in microstructure_notes. Sandwich rows carry the fibre face-sheet description in additional_fillers; their properties are panel-level, not core-level. Rows from Tables 6.2 and 7.2 quoting other authors are marked secondary and carry the citation in sample_label; the series/parallel/Hirsch predictions of Tables 8.7-8.8 are marked model. Test 'strain rate' quoted in the thesis (50 mm/mm tensile, 5 mm/mm flexural) is not a strain rate, so strain_rate_per_s is left null; tests were at room temperature (taken as 25 C).

extraction.paper_summary: Review article (Pranesh et al., Maritime Technology and Research 2023) surveying the mechanical features of eight deep-sea human occupied vehicles (Alvin, Jiaolong, MIR-1/MIR-2, Nautile, Shinkai 6500, Deep Sea Challenger, Fendouzhe, Triton): pressure hulls, hatches, ballast and trim systems, exo-structures, pressure vessels, drop weights and syntactic foam. Syntactic foam is covered in one short section (4.6): it is described as a polymer, metal or ceramic matrix filled with cenosphere, glass, carbon or polymer micro-balloons, and Table 8 lists the as-used buoyancy-foam density for five of the vehicles (500-700 kg/m3), with the review concluding that ~500 kg/m3 foam suits deep-water and ~700 kg/m3 foam ultra-deep (full-ocean-depth) service. No mechanical property data for syntactic foams are reported.

extraction.extraction_notes: BORDERLINE ON-TOPIC. This is a naval-engineering review of human occupied vehicles, not a syntactic-foam materials study; syntactic foam is only one of eight subsystems reviewed (Sec. 4.6). It is marked is_syntactic_foam_paper=true because it does contain extractable hollow-particle-composite data - Table 8, the as-used buoyancy-foam density of five submersibles - but a reviewer may reasonably prefer to reclassify it as off-topic and drop the records. All five records are data_origin='secondary': every Table 8 value is quoted from other publications (Bernstein 1967; Hardy et al. 2014; Jamieson et al. 2019; Momma 1999; Pan et al. 2012) and the individual citation could not be attributed per row, so the full citation list is carried in sample_label. Unit conversion: kg/m3 -> g/cm3 (divided by 1000): Alvin 500->0.5, Jiaolong 526->0.526, Shinkai 6500 536->0.536, Deep Sea Challenger 700->0.7, Triton 625->0.625. MIR-1/MIR-2, Nautile and Fendouzhe rows of Table 8 are '---' (unknown) and were skipped. No mechanical properties (modulus, strength, hydrostatic collapse), no microballoon volume fraction, grade, size or matrix system are reported for any foam, so all Properties fields and most Processing fields are null; matrix_class/particle_type are 'other' except for Deep Sea Challenger, where the text explicitly says the foam is 'a combination of epoxy resins and glass spheres'. test_type is 'other' because no mechanical test underlies these numbers. The summary statement that 'the density of syntactic foam ranges from 500 to 700 kg/m3' (conclusion 7) is a range over the same Table 8 values and was not duplicated as a separate record. All other tables in the paper (pressure hull materials/thicknesses, ballast, trim, exo-structure, drop weights, W/D ratios, vehicle specifications) concern non-foam subsystems and are outside the schema.

extraction.paper_summary: Kazymyrenko, Solomoniuk and Drozd (Polish Maritime Research 30(3), 2023, 174-180) study binder-free hot-press sintering of hollow glass microspheres (Na2O-SiO2 sodium silicate and Na2O-B2O3-SiO2 sodium borosilicate, 10-60 um diameter, 0.5-2.0 um wall) into closed-cell 'glass composites' for underwater buoyancy modules, positioned as a polymer-free analogue of syntactic foams. Sintering at 650-700 C under 0.5-1.5 MPa densifies the powder from 250-270 kg/m3 in the green state to 350-600 kg/m3, with up to 50% linear shrinkage and 20-25% shell deformation. Samples of 320, 400 and 500 kg/m3 were tested for water absorption under hydrostatic pressure to 20 MPa and for microsphere destruction to 45 MPa, and their sound-pressure attenuation was measured in a Kundt tube; all of these results are presented only as figures with no tabulated numbers.

records.sample_label: Sintered hollow-glass-microsphere composite, apparent density 320 kg/m3 (Fig. 8 curve 1)

processing.matrix_name: No matrix / binder: the continuous phase is formed by viscous flow and contact sintering of the microsphere walls themselves (hot pressing of bulk microspheres without plasticisers or additives in a sealed graphite container)
processing.particle_grade: Sodium silicate glass Na2O-SiO2 (77.0 wt% SiO2, 23.0 wt% Na2O) and/or sodium borosilicate glass Na2O-B2O3-SiO2 (69.0 SiO2, 7.5 B2O3, 6.0 CaO, 13.5 Na2O, 2.0 ZnO, 2.0 F wt%)

structure.microstructure_notes: Predominantly closed-porous cellular structure with both closed and open pores between sintered microspheres; open porosity aids sound insulation while closed porosity reduces water absorption. Microsphere shells deform 20-25% of original size; shape factor (min/max particle size) falls from 1.0 to 0.75; contact-area perimeter 30-50 um. Linear shrinkage during sintering reaches up to 50%. Powder density before sintering 250-270 kg/m3. Precursor microspheres 10-60 um diameter with 0.5-2.0 um shell thickness.

test.specimen_notes: All-round hydrostatic loading in a distilled-water chamber at 2, 5, 15 and 20 MPa; loading rate 0.01 MPa/s, hold 3-5 min per level; water absorption measured by hydrostatic weighing after each loading, relative error within +/-5%. Water-absorption values appear only in Fig. 8 with no numeric values in text or tables.

evidence.quote: Figure 8 shows the graphical dependence of the water absorption values of samples with densities of 320 kg/m3 (curve 1), 400 kg/m3 (curve 2), and 500 kg/m3 (curve 3) under conditions of gradual loading with all-round hydrostatic pressure.

The sample was subjected to hydrostatic pressures of 2, 5, 15, and 20 MPa, and the exposure of the pressure time was 3 - 5 min at a rate of 0.01 MPa/s. The water absorption was determined by hydrostatic weighing after each loading; the relative error in the measurements did not exceed ± 5 %.

structure.microstructure_notes: Predominantly closed-porous cellular structure formed by viscous glass-phase flow; higher pressing pressure gives more intense sintering and higher density. Precursor microspheres 10-60 um diameter with 0.5-2.0 um shell thickness.

test.specimen_notes: All-round hydrostatic loading in distilled water at 2, 5, 15 and 20 MPa; 0.01 MPa/s, hold 3-5 min; water absorption by hydrostatic weighing, error within +/-5%. Values only in Fig. 8.

evidence.quote: Figure 8 shows the graphical dependence of the water absorption values of samples with densities of 320 kg/m3 (curve 1), 400 kg/m3 (curve 2), and 500 kg/m3 (curve 3) under conditions of gradual loading with all-round hydrostatic pressure.

It was established that the formation of a predominantly closed-porous structure of glass composites with a density of 350...600 kg/m3 occurs by the mechanisms of viscous glass phase flow through liquefaction processes in the walls of microspheres. At the same time, shrinkage processes in the linear direction reach up to 50%.

extraction.extraction_notes: BORDERLINE ON-TOPIC. The material is built entirely from hollow glass microspheres, but it has NO matrix phase: the microspheres are hot-pressed and sintered together without any binder, plasticiser or additive, so the continuous phase is the sintered microsphere glass itself. The authors present it as a polymer-free competitor/analogue to syntactic foams ('The absence of a polymeric binder helps to obtain lightweight compositions whose density is 20% lower than syntactic foams with glass microspheres') and call the specimens 'syntactic glass' in the Fig. 4 caption. It was flagged is_syntactic_foam_paper=true because it is genuinely hollow-particle-based, but matrix_class was set to 'other' with an explanatory matrix_name, process_route to 'other' (binder-free hot-press sintering in a sealed graphite container), and particle_volume_fraction was left NULL rather than set to 1.0, because after sintering there is no meaningful particle/matrix volume split. Downstream users should treat these records as a sintered hollow-microsphere cellular glass, not as a matrix-filled syntactic foam. NO NUMERIC PROPERTY VALUES EXIST IN THIS PAPER. There is not a single table; every result - sintering kinetics/shrinkage (Fig. 6), sound pressure level in octave bands (Fig. 7), water absorption vs hydrostatic pressure (Fig. 8) and per-cent of destroyed microspheres Np vs hydrostatic pressure from 5 to 45 MPa (Fig. 9) - is presented only as a plot, so modulus, strength, water/moisture uptake and all other property fields are null in every record. The only quantitative sample-level data are the three apparent densities (320, 400 and 500 kg/m3 = 0.32, 0.40, 0.50 g/cm3, converted by dividing by 1000) named in the Fig. 8 text, which is why exactly three records were created. Other quantitative statements recorded in notes rather than fields: green (pre-sintering) powder density 250-270 kg/m3; sintered density range 350-600 kg/m3 (abstract) and 320-500 kg/m3 for the acoustic samples; microsphere diameter 10-60 um and shell thickness 0.5-2.0 um (a true density and a radius ratio eta could be estimated from these but are not stated, so both fields are null); sintering at 650 C isothermal (700 C quoted in the abstract as the upper criterion) at 0.5, 1.0, 1.2 and 1.5 MPa; sintering lasts 25-30 min and is most intense in the first 8 min; shrinkage starts at 550 C for Na2O-SiO2 and 500 C for Na2O-B2O3-SiO2 glasses; linear shrinkage up to 50%; shell deformation 20-25%; shape factor 1.0 -> 0.75; contact perimeter 30-50 um. The two glass chemistries (Na2O-SiO2 vs Na2O-B2O3-SiO2) are compared in Figs. 6 and 9 but no density or property number is attributed to either system individually, so the three records list both compositions in particle_grade instead of being split by glass system. Literature comparison values quoted in the introduction were NOT turned into secondary records because they are ranges for whole material classes rather than measurements of specific samples: syntactic foams 450-700 kg/m3 with operating depth to 12,000 m [ref 14]; foam glass 300-700 kg/m3 from 20-150 um powders, depth to 2000 m [ref 15]; polyurethane foam about 100 kg/m3, maximum depth 350 m, upper service temperature 60 C; syntactic-foam service-temperature limit 110-130 C.

extraction.paper_summary: Journal of Advanced Zoology 44(S-3), 2023, pp. 1654-1661 (page footers read 1259-1267): a Taguchi L9 / ANOVA study of the ultimate tensile strength (ASTM C297, 120 x 34 x 17 mm specimens) of Kevlar/jute/foam hybrid SANDWICH composites, varying skin material (jute+jute, jute+Kevlar, Kevlar+Kevlar), a 'density' factor (40/60/80) and reinforcement percentage (25/50/75%). Ultimate tensile strength ranged from 44 to 61 MPa, was highest for Kevlar+Kevlar skins, and ANOVA found skin material (F=10.30, p=0.088) and density (F=6.29, p=0.137) more influential than reinforcement percentage (F=3.13, p=0.242). Despite the title's use of 'syntactic foam', the core the authors actually fabricated is described in the materials section as 'Synthetic foam core material (e.g., polyurethane foam)' - a conventional blown foam - and no hollow filler particles are used anywhere in the experimental work.
extraction.extraction_notes: Marked off-topic (is_syntactic_foam_paper=false, no records) under rule 6, for the following reasons. (1) No hollow-particle filler is used by the authors. Sec. 2.1 states 'Synthetic foam core material (e.g., polyurethane foam) of specified density variations were used as main material', i.e. a conventional polymer foam core, not a hollow-particle-filled composite. Microballoons, microspheres, cenospheres and 'hollow-particle filled' appear ONLY in the introduction's literature review and in the reference list (refs 3, 18, 19, 21) - never in the authors' own materials, fabrication or results. (2) The paper conflates 'syntactic' and 'synthetic' throughout (title says 'Syntactic Foam', abstract and keywords say 'synthetic foam'), and the materials list even calls the core 'syntactic foam (Synthetic fiber) of density 1.096 g/cm3', which is internally incoherent. There is no particle grade, particle size, wall thickness, particle density or particle volume/weight fraction anywhere. (3) The work is a sandwich-panel study (Kevlar and/or jute face sheets bonded with LY556 epoxy adhesive to a foam core), i.e. a generic composite/sandwich paper rather than a hollow-particle composite paper. (4) The reported factor values are not physically interpretable as material densities: the 'Density (gm/cm3)' column of Tables 1 and 2 takes values 40, 60 and 80 g/cc, and the text repeats '40 g/cc, 60 g/cc, 80 g/cc' for the SKIN materials, which is impossible for jute or Kevlar (the same section separately gives Kevlar 1.450 g/cm3, jute 1.500 g/cm3, foam 1.096 g/cm3, resin 1.150 g/cm3). The units are evidently wrong or the factor is something other than density, so these values could not be mapped to the schema even if the paper were in scope. For reference, the tensile data that WOULD have been extractable is Table 2: jute+jute 44 / 51 / 52 MPa, jute+Kevlar 50.5 / 54 / 55 MPa, Kevlar+Kevlar 56 / 52.5 / 61 MPa at the nine Taguchi conditions; only ultimate tensile strength is reported (no modulus values are given despite being mentioned in the abstract, and Figures 5 and 6 - main effect plots for means and SN ratios - are images).

extraction.paper_summary: Pados et al. produced AlSi7Mg aluminium matrix syntactic foams (MMSFs) by pressurised (500 kPa argon) infiltration of Liapor lightweight expanded clay aggregate particles (LECAPs, sieved to 2.5-3.0 mm), then machined ~26 mm diameter, 160 mm long cores and either left them bare, inserted them into heat-treated AlMgSi0.5 tubes (32 mm OD, 2 mm wall), or adhesively bonded them into the tubes with 3M Scotch-Weld DP410 epoxy. Quasi-static three-point bend tests (ISO 7438:2020, 140 mm span, 5 mm/min) up to 25 mm deflection showed flexural strengths of 69 MPa (bare MMSF), 159 MPa (foam-filled tube) and 169 MPa (adhesive-bonded foam-filled tube), i.e. the epoxy-bonded tubes gained 6% over unbonded foam-filled tubes and 145% over bare MMSFs. The foam cores had an average density of 1.48 +/- 0.05 g/cm3, roughly half that of the aluminium alloy.

extraction.extraction_notes:
Three records: one per specimen configuration (bare MMSF, foam-filled tube, adhesive-bonded foam-filled tube). All share the same syntactic foam composition and the same three-point bend test condition; the 12 individual specimens are replicates, so properties are only published as per-type averages (Table 2) and are entered once per type.

Particle type: the filler is Liapor lightweight expanded clay aggregate (LECAP), a porous/cellular expanded-clay ceramic granule (~60 wt% SiO2, ~17 wt% Al2O3, ~14 wt% Fe2O3), mapped to 'ceramic_hollow' as the closest enum; it is not a thin-walled hollow microsphere, so treat the classification with care.

Nulls: particle volume/weight fraction, particle true density, wall-thickness ratio and mean diameter are not reported in this paper (the filler was characterised in ref. [27]). Only the sieved size range 2.5-3.0 mm is given, so particle_mean_diameter_um is left null rather than assuming a midpoint. No modulus is reported. Strain at failure is left null: the paper reports deflections (e.g. bare MMSF fractures at ~2 mm deflection), not strains.

Energy absorption: Table 2 reports absorbed energy in joules at 5, 10, 15, 20 and 25 mm deflection (f-MMSF: 29, 91, 136, 143, 144 J; f-EMMSF: 36, 107, 139, 145, 148 J; MMSF: 6 J at all deflections; ET: 23, 61, 102, 142, 179 J). These are total absorbed energies for a bend specimen, not volumetric MJ/m3, and cannot be converted without an assumed deformed volume, so energy_absorption_mj_m3 is left null.

Density: measured_density_g_cc is set to the study-wide foam-core average of 1.48 +/- 0.05 g/cm3 explicitly stated in Sec. 2.2; individual specimen and core densities from Table 1 are listed in microstructure_notes. Note that Table 1 labels both bare-foam specimens 'MMSF_1' (densities 1.42 and 1.60 g/cm3); the second is presumably MMSF_2.

Process temperature: left null because the paper gives a range rather than a single value - crucible and LECAPs preheated at 600 C for >=30 min, AlSi7Mg heated to ~850 C, and the melt poured and infiltrated at 750-800 C under 500 kPa argon pressure.

Test temperature: not stated; set to 25 C on the standard room-temperature assumption for these quasi-static laboratory bend tests.

Excluded: the empty AlMgSi0.5 tube reference specimens (ET, flexural strength 90 +/- 1 MPa, Fmax 4064 +/- 90 N, 179 J at 25 mm) contain no hollow particles and are not a syntactic foam composition, so no record was created for them. Literature values cited in the introduction (refs. [9], [14], [16], [24], [25], [26]) are qualitative or percentage comparisons with no extractable absolute property values, so no secondary records were created.

Evidence quotes from Table 2 are reconstructed across the line-per-cell layout of the extracted text (the source file lists each cell on its own line) and use 'sigma_b' and '+/-' for the sigma and plus-minus characters.

extraction.paper_summary: Archaeological conservation study of a Late Period Egyptian polychrome wooden coffin from Dahshur: the object was characterised by optical/stereo/digital microscopy, 2D and photogrammetric 3D documentation, SEM-EDX, XRD and wood anatomy (yellow layer = goethite/yellow ochre, ground layer = calcite plus gypsum, textile = linen plain weave, wood = Ficus sycomorus and Quercus cerris). Conservation comprised mechanical and chemical cleaning (xylene/distilled water 1:1 on the black resin layer, ethyl alcohol/water on the painted layer), reassembly with beech dowels and Paraloid B72 (15 % and 50 %), gap filling with cotton and with glass microballoons in Paraloid B72 (15 %), and consolidation of the painted layer with nano-silica in Klucel G (0.5 %). No hollow-particle composite was fabricated or mechanically characterised.
extraction.extraction_notes: Off-topic for the syntactic-foam database. The only hollow-particle material mentioned is a commercial 'glass microballoon' filler paste mixed with Paraloid B72 (15 % in acetone) that was used to level losses and cracks in the coffin before retouching ('After complete drying, a glass microballoon was used in paraloid B72 (15%) to level the surface and prepare for the colouring process of the completed parts', Loss Compensation section; Figs. 19, 21, 22). No microballoon grade, size, density, volume or weight fraction is given, and the paper reports no mechanical, thermal or physical property measurement of that filler or of any composite - a keyword sweep of the whole file finds no MPa/GPa, modulus, strength, density or fraction values anywhere. All quantitative numbers in the paper concern the object (190 x 51 x 55 cm coffin, 15 cm dowel), instrument settings (SEM 30 kV; XRD 40 kV / 30 mA), wood anatomy (vessel lumina 100-200 um and >200 um) and reagent concentrations (Paraloid B72 15 % / 50 %, Klucel G 1 % and 0.5 %, nano-silica in Klucel G 0.5 %). Therefore is_syntactic_foam_paper=false and records=[] per rule 6/10.

extraction.paper_summary: Phenolic (phenol-formaldehyde) syntactic foam filled with dry fly ash cenospheres (50:50 proportion, 0.70 reinforcement volume fraction by resin burnout) was used as the core of glass/epoxy faced sandwich panels, either plain (SF) or confined in honeycomb grid cells of 20, 15, 10 and 5 mm (SFK20-SFK5). Tensile, compressive, flexural (long and short beam) and three-rail shear properties were measured in flatwise (out-of-plane) and edgewise (in-plane) configurations per ASTM standards. Confining the foam in the honeycomb grid raised the mechanical properties by 20-180%, with the smallest (5 mm) cell size best; the phenolic foam was thermally stable to 450 C.

extraction.extraction_notes: All moduli were reported in GPa and converted to MPa (x1000). Properties are those of the sandwich panel (syntactic foam core + glass/epoxy face skins), not of the bare foam; the honeycomb grid and face skins are recorded in additional_fillers. particle_volume_fraction=0.70 is the reinforcement volume fraction of the syntactic foam from the resin burnout test (Table 1); the text also states a 50:50 foam mixing proportion, which is not explicitly labelled as weight or volume, so particle_weight_fraction was left null. Test temperature was not stated (ambient assumed but left null). Strain rate was not reported; only a constant crosshead displacement rate of 0.5 mm/min is given, and no gauge length is provided to convert it, so strain_rate_per_s is null. Strain at failure, density and energy absorption are only visible in stress-strain figures (Figs. 2-6) and are not tabulated, so they are left null. Long-beam and short-beam flexure are distinguished in test.specimen_notes. process_route recorded as vacuum_assisted because the resin-impregnated glass fabrics were vacuum bonded to the packed foam core.

extraction.paper_summary: A theoretical/modelling paper that assembles existing micromechanics models (Gibson-Ashby for resin-impregnated paper honeycomb, Porfiri and Gupta's differential scheme for syntactic foam, and rule-of-mixtures/Halpin-Tsai for woven E-glass/epoxy face skins) into a modified classical lamination theory (MCLT) for foam-core sandwich composites. For the syntactic foam (dry fly ash cenospheres, mean diameter 150 um, radius ratio eta = 0.9, Vceno = 0.7272 in a phenolic resin matrix) the predicted Young's modulus is 1.99 GPa, Poisson's ratio 0.25, shear modulus 0.796 GPa and density 654.54 kg/m3. The MCLT predictions for the syntactic-foam-core / E-glass-epoxy-skin sandwich (Ex = Ey = 4.469 GPa, Gxy = 1.0023 GPa, Gyz = Gxz = 0.9838 GPa) agree with experimental values reported earlier by Amith Kumar S.J. and Sabeel Ahmed within 1.9-5.2%.

extraction.extraction_notes: This is a purely analytical/review paper: no material was made or tested here, so no record is 'primary'. Model predictions are data_origin='model'; the experimental columns in Tables 6-7 are values reported earlier by the authors in ref [3] (Amith Kumar S.J., Sabeel Ahmed K., J. Reinforced Plastics and Composites 2013, 32, 1370-1379) and are therefore data_origin='secondary' with the citation in sample_label. CAVEAT on records 3-8: these are properties of the SANDWICH PANEL (syntactic foam core between woven E-glass/epoxy skins), not of the bare syntactic foam, so their moduli must not be read as foam moduli; sample_label flags this and the cenosphere volume fraction / core density fields were deliberately left null on those records (the fraction applies to the core only). Only records 1-2 describe the bare syntactic foam. Excluded from records: the resin-impregnated paper honeycomb core (Tables 1-3, samples N20/K20/K15/K10/K5) and the E-glass/epoxy face skin (Tables 5-6), because neither is a hollow-particle composite. Unit conversions: GPa x 1000 -> MPa (1.99 -> 1990, 0.796 -> 796, 4.469 -> 4469, 4.38 -> 4380, 1.0023 -> 1002.3, 0.961 -> 961, 0.9838 -> 983.8, 1.035 -> 1035); kg/m3 / 1000 -> g/cm3 (654.54 -> 0.65454 foam density, 450 -> 0.45 cenosphere true density). Ex = Ey and Gyz = Gxz in Table 7, so one record each rather than duplicates. Foam Poisson's ratio 0.25 (misprinted as '0.25 GPa' in the text) has no schema field and is kept in microstructure_notes. No strength, strain, energy-absorption or thermal data appear anywhere in the paper. Process route is 'other' because no fabrication route is described for the modelled foam.

extraction.paper_summary: Matrix-less (binderless) syntactic foam was produced by spark plasma sintering fly-ash cenospheres (fractions 63-150 um and 150-250 um) in 20, 30 and 50 mm graphite dies at 1050-1300 C under ~0.6 kN (1.9 MPa in the 20 mm die). Sintering shrinkage starts near 900 C; apparent density rises with sintering temperature (e.g. 0.97 -> 2.3 g/cm3 for CS 63-150 um in a 20 mm die between 1050 and 1300 C) while total porosity falls from 61.5 % to 3.9 % (1050-1250 C). Compressive strength of the CS 63-150 um / 20 mm die series rises from 11 MPa to 312 MPa over 1050-1300 C, following the Rice porosity model with an extrapolated fully dense strength of 411.1 MPa.

extraction.extraction_notes: Matrix-less syntactic foam: cenospheres are sintered directly to each other with no matrix, so matrix_class is set to 'other' with matrix_name explaining there is no matrix, and particle_weight_fraction = 1.0 (the material is 100 wt% cenospheres, stated as 'matrix-less SF foam containing CS only'). process_route 'powder_metallurgy' is used for spark plasma sintering (Dr. Sinter SPS825, ~0.6 kN = 1.9 MPa in the 20 mm die, 6 Pa vacuum). cure_or_process_temperature_c holds the sintering temperature. Almost all numeric data in this paper are only in figures (Figs. 2-20); the only values stated numerically in text are the abstract/conclusions endpoints, so records exist only for the lowest and highest sintering temperature of each series and intermediate points were left out rather than read off plots. Total porosity (61.5 % at 1050 C down to 3.9 % at 1250 C) and open porosity (0.28-43 %) are the porosity of the whole matrix-less foam (inter-particle plus intra-cenosphere void), not unintended matrix porosity, so they are recorded in microstructure_notes rather than in matrix_porosity_fraction. Pre-sintering cenosphere breakage: 3 % in the 50 mm die is unambiguous and recorded; the 20 mm die CS 63-150 um numbers ('21 % and 20 %, respectively') and the CS 150-250 um numbers (23 % plus an additional 37 %) are ambiguous/cumulative and are only described in notes. Compressive strength test temperature is not stated (assumed ambient but left null); no strain rate, modulus or strain data are reported. The chemical composition table (Table 1) is a literature compilation, not measurements of these cenospheres, so no record was made from it.

extraction.paper_summary: Persian-language study (Loghman et al., Advanced Materials in Engineering 43(1), 2024) on vinyl ester / hollow glass microballoon syntactic foams. Pure VE-200 vinyl ester resin and foams with 20, 40 and 60 vol% silane-treated H38H glass microballoons (true density 0.38 g/cm3) were cast in silicone moulds, cured at room temperature and post-cured at 80 C for 3 h. Density fell from 1.04 to 0.56 g/cm3 while compressive strength fell from 80 to 55 MPa and tensile strength from 45 to 17 MPa; specific compressive strength rose from 76.9 to 98.2 MPa.cm3/g. Results are compared in Table 6 with Gupta et al. (Compos. B Eng. 2010) vinyl ester foams made with 0.32 g/cm3 microballoons.

extraction.extraction_notes: PAPER IS IN PERSIAN; the PDF text layer is right-to-left reversed, so Persian decimal numbers appear as '04 /1' meaning 1.04 and '15 /0±' meaning +/-0.15. All decodings were cross-checked arithmetically: Table 6 modulus/density = Table 6 specific modulus, and Table 6 strength/Table 5 density = Table 5 specific strength, and they agree to rounding for every present-study row, which confirms the column mapping. UNITS: GPa moduli from Table 6 converted to MPa (x1000); specific moduli converted from GPa.cm3/g to MPa.cm3/g (x1000). Vol% converted to fractions. CAVEATS: (1) The abstract states the highest tensile strength (neat resin) is 40 MPa while Table 6 lists 45 +/- 2.9 MPa; the table value was used since it is internally consistent with the Table 5 specific tensile strength of 43.2 MPa.cm3/g. (2) Table 5's 'theoretical density' column (0.878/0.784/0.690/0.596 g/cm3) is lower than the measured density for the 0, 20 and 40 vol% samples, so the paper's void formula (rho_T - rho_ex)/rho_T yields NEGATIVE porosity for those three rows even though the table prints the magnitudes 18.4%, 12.2% and 1.4%. The theoretical densities are recorded as printed, but matrix_porosity_fraction is left null for 0/20/40 vol% and only recorded (0.0604) for the 60 vol% sample where the value is genuinely positive. A theoretical density of 0.878 g/cm3 for neat vinyl ester is also inconsistent with the stated resin density of 1.13 g/cm3 (Table 3), so this column looks unreliable. (3) Table 5 also contains three columns of Gupta-group data (specific compressive strength 73.0/80.3/83.0/85.1 MPa.cm3/g, matrix void 4.4/7.3/6.8/8.9%, density 0.869/0.765/0.690/0.597 g/cm3), but those rows cannot be aligned unambiguously with the Gupta compositions (30/40/50/60 vol%) listed in Table 6 - the products do not reproduce the Table 6 strengths - so they were NOT attached to the secondary records. (4) Gupta secondary rows from Table 6 are also internally inconsistent (modulus / specific modulus implies densities of ~0.91, 0.85, 0.81/0.71, 0.91/0.80 g/cm3 for compression vs tension), and the tensile strengths of 8 and 7 MPa at 50 and 60 vol% may be OCR-truncated; these records were given low extractor_confidence. (5) Batch masses are 100 g resin + 0/10/22/40 g microballoons (Table 4); particle_weight_fraction was left null because the catalyst/accelerator masses are given only as volumes so an exact weight fraction cannot be formed. (6) Strain rate was not stated; only the crosshead rate of 1 mm/min (0.1 mm/min in the cited Gupta work) is given, so strain_rate_per_s is null and the crosshead rate is recorded in specimen_notes. Test temperature is never stated, so temperature_c is null. (7) Plateau stress, energy absorption, densification strain and strain at failure appear only in the stress-strain plots of Figs. 5 and 7 with no numeric values in text or tables, so they are left null. (8) Particle mean diameter 45 um is the D50 from Table 1 (D90 = 85 um); Table 1 also gives a microballoon crush strength of 31 MPa and a density range of 0.36-0.40 g/cm3 around the nominal 0.38 g/cm3.

extraction.paper_summary: Aluminium 2024 matrix syntactic foams were made by vacuum casting (-1 bar vacuum, 560 C, then 15 bar argon pressure, three-step mould filling with vibration) around packed beds of three low-cost lightweight porous aggregates sieved to 2.5-4.5 mm: expanded perlite, LECA (expanded clay) and pumice. Foam densities were 1.09, 1.385 and 2.05 g/cm3 with aggregate volume fractions of 66.8, 62.8 and 50.0% and total porosities of 62.6, 50.5 and 33.2%. Quasi-static uniaxial compression (ISO 13314) gave plateau stresses of 14.12, 19.31 and 31.1 MPa, unloading moduli of 3.97, 6.19 and 7.2 GPa, densification strains of 65, 69 and 60%, energy absorption of 5.4, 11.2 and 17.5 MJ/m3 and energy absorption efficiencies of 66, 70.5 and 79% at 50% strain; compressive properties and energy absorption rose with density, and low-density foams failed in a shear band while high-density pumice foam deformed uniformly.

structure.microstructure_notes: Total porosity of the foam F_TP = 62.55% (Table 3); the expanded perlite particles themselves are about 92% porous with a solid-phase density of 2.81 g/cm3. Aggregates are evenly distributed with a distinct boundary to the matrix; aluminium did not penetrate the aggregate cavities and no debonding was seen. Table 3 lists the foam density as 1.09 g/cm3. This lower-density foam deformed locally along a large shear band.

extraction.extraction_notes: PRIMARY DATA (3 records): from Table 3 (physical) and Table 4 (mechanical). modulus_mpa is the unloading elastic modulus E_UL (GPa x 1000); the quasi-elastic gradient QE is given in test.specimen_notes because the schema has only one modulus field. plateau_stress_mpa is sigma_Pl (ISO 13314 mean stress over 20-40% strain); sigma_Ple (= 1.3 x sigma_Pl, 18.36 / 25.10 / 40.43 MPa) is a derived quantity and was not stored, and no sigma_max was reported for the authors' own samples, so strength_mpa is null for the primary records. densification_strain is epsilon_Ple converted from % to fraction (0.65 / 0.69 / 0.60). INCONSISTENCIES IN THE PAPER: (a) the abstract states energy absorption efficiencies of 85 / 78 / 70% for perlite / LECA / pumice, which contradicts Table 4 and the conclusion (66 / 70.5 / 79%); the Table 4 values were used. (b) the abstract calls 0.24, 0.55 and 1.30 g/cm3 the foam densities, but Table 3 shows these are the aggregate densities and the foam densities are 1.09, 1.35 and 2.05 g/cm3. (c) the LECA foam density is 1.35 in Table 3 and 1.385 in Table 4; Table 4 was used for measured_density_g_cc and Table 3 is noted in microstructure_notes. (d) particle size is given as 2.5-4.5 mm in Sec. 3.1 but 4.75-6.30 mm on p. 7; because of that conflict and because no mean was stated, particle_mean_diameter_um was left null. particle_true_density_g_cc holds the aggregate (particle) density from Table 3; the skeletal/solid-phase densities (2.81, 2.95, 3.6 g/cm3) and the particle porosities (92, 80, 64%) are in microstructure_notes. The total foam porosity F_TP was NOT put in matrix_porosity_fraction because that field means unintended matrix voids, whereas F_TP here is the intended aggregate porosity; it is recorded in microstructure_notes. Test temperature and strain rate were not stated (only 'quasi-static'), so both are null. SECONDARY DATA (16 records): 14 rows of Table 1 (a literature comparison table) plus two values quoted in the introduction (Bonabi et al. ref. 29 and Taherishargh et al. ref. 31); all are marked data_origin=secondary with the cited reference in sample_label. Table 1 was not machine-parsed into a [TABLE] block in the text file, so its evidence quotes are the row values reassembled in column order from the linearised text. Manufacturing routes without a matching enum value (gravity infiltration casting, pressureless infiltration, melt infiltration, DMD, counter-gravity casting) were mapped to process_route='other' and named in specimen_notes / microstructure_notes. CAVEAT ON PARTICLE TYPE: perlite, LECA and pumice are porous (non-hollow, irregular) lightweight aggregates rather than true hollow microspheres, so particle_type='other' was used for them; the paper nevertheless classifies the resulting materials as metal matrix syntactic foams.

extraction.paper_summary: In situ synchrotron X-ray micro-computed tomography combined with generative adversarial network (GAN) super-resolution was used to track the microstructural evolution of two superlight ablator (SLA) syntactic foams - SLA-220 (silicone elastomer + silica microballoons + silica fibers) and SLA-561V (silicone elastomer + silica and phenolic microballoons + cork filler + glass/carbon fibers) - during pyrolysis to 900 C at 15 C/min in inert atmosphere. The study quantifies constituent solid volume fractions, open/closed/total porosity, envelope volume change and tortuosity as a function of temperature, and relates them to TGA decomposition chemistry. SLA-220 shrank 12% and became more tortuous with a 70-75% char yield, while SLA-561V swelled ~5% early, then shrank 32% from 450-900 C, with a 50% char yield and a large increase in open porosity caused by volatilization of the cork phase.

extraction.extraction_notes: On-topic (hollow-particle syntactic foams: silica and phenolic microballoons in a silicone elastomer matrix) but the paper contains NO mechanical or thermophysical property measurements - it is a microstructure/pyrolysis imaging study. All Properties fields are therefore null; records capture composition, density and porosity/degradation structure only. test_type is set to 'other' (in situ synchrotron micro-CT during pyrolysis + TGA), with temperature_c = 23 for the virgin state and 900 for the fully charred state. matrix_class 'other_thermoset' is used for the silicone elastomer matrix; process_route 'other' because the proprietary manufacturing route (Lockheed Martin) is not described. For SLA-561V, particle_volume_fraction/particle_weight_fraction give the silica microballoon phase only (43.9 bulk vol%, 35.1 mass%) to stay consistent with particle_type = glass_microballoon and particle_true_density = 0.18 g/cm3; the phenolic microballoons, cork and fibers are listed in additional_fillers, and the paper states the combined silica + phenolic microballoon bulk volume fraction is ~58%. The nominal compositions in Tables 1 and 2 (including the total densities 0.250 and 0.225 g/cm3) are cited by the authors from Strauss, 'Low density ablator compositions', US patent 4031059 (ref. 45); the porosity, volume fraction, envelope volume, tortuosity and char yield values are the authors' own measurements, so records are marked primary. Note an internal inconsistency in the paper: the SLA-220 char yield is given as 70% on page 2 and 75% on page 3 - both are recorded in the notes. Absolute charred densities were not stated (only 85% and 74% of virgin for SLA-220 and SLA-561V), so measured_density_g_cc is left null for the charred records rather than back-calculated. Tortuosity factors, per-phase solid volume fraction vs temperature, surface areas and RMSE values appear only in Figs. 3-8 and were not read off the plots. The class-level statements 'low density (<0.3 g/cm3), low thermal conductivity (<0.5 W/m/K)' in the introduction describe SLA materials generically and were not entered as measured values.

extraction.paper_summary: Epoxy (bis-A / cycloaliphatic amine) syntactic foams filled with K15 glass-clad hollow silica microballoons (40 um mean diameter, 0.15 g/cm3 bulk density) at 10-50 vol% were cast under vacuum in a planetary centrifugal mixer and characterised for density, total/effective porosity (density-based and SEM area analysis) and three-point flexural performance per ASTM D790. Density fell nearly linearly from 1.15 g/cm3 (neat epoxy) to 0.63 g/cm3 at 50 vol%, while total porosity rose from 2.7% to 18.4% and effective (interconnected) porosity from 0.9% to 13.6%, with a sharp percolation jump above 30 vol%. Flexural strength and modulus peaked at 30 vol% (96 MPa, 3.12 GPa) and then dropped sharply at 40-50 vol% because of microballoon agglomeration, shell collapse and interstitial voids.
