extraction.extraction_notes: Short journal paper with no data tables; all numeric values come from text/abstract statements about Figures 1-3. Records were created only for the loadings whose values are stated numerically (0, 30, 40, 50 vol%). The 10 and 20 vol% specimens were fabricated and appear in Figures 1-3, but no numeric density, porosity or flexural values are given for them, so they were omitted rather than read off the plots. Unit conversions: flexural modulus GPa -> MPa (2.69 GPa = 2690 MPa; 3.12 GPa = 3120 MPa); porosity percentages -> fractions (2.7% = 0.027, 18.4% = 0.184). Total porosity P_t (density-based, (rho_th - rho_exp)/rho_th) was mapped to structure.matrix_porosity_fraction and the SEM-derived effective porosity P_e recorded in microstructure_notes; note that in this paper P_t also includes the intended hollow-microballoon void volume, so it is not purely unintended matrix porosity. Values that are derivable but not stated were left null and are noted here: the 30 vol% density (abstract states a 28% reduction from 1.15 g/cm3, i.e. ~0.83 g/cm3) and the 50 vol% flexural strength/modulus (stated 35% and 33% drops from the 96 MPa / 3.12 GPa peak, i.e. ~62 MPa and ~2.09 GPa). Particle 'bulk density 0.15 g/cm3' was reported for K15 but is a bulk (tapped) density, not a true particle density, so particle_true_density_g_cc was left null. Test temperature taken as the 23 +/- 2 C conditioning/lab temperature; cross-head rate 1 mm/min was not converted to a strain rate. Cure was 24 h at room temperature plus 2 h post-cure at 60 C; 60 C recorded as the process temperature.

extraction.paper_summary: Mahesh (2025) fabricates epoxy (Lapox L12/K6) syntactic foams filled with 20, 40 and 60 vol% fly-ash cenospheres (CIL 100, SFC series) or recycled rubber crumb (CRMB60, SFR series) by room-temperature mechanical mixing and casting, and compares them with neat epoxy under ASTM D7136 drop-weight low-velocity impact at 39.62, 79.02 and 118.82 J. Rubber-crumb foams absorb the most total energy (SFR60: 16.75 J at 118.82 J impact vs 6.46 J for neat epoxy) via viscoelastic/ductile mechanisms, while the lower-density cenosphere foams give the highest specific energy absorption (SFC60: 0.0115 Jm3/kg, +117% over neat epoxy). Density falls from 1210 kg/m3 (neat epoxy) to 1005 kg/m3 (SFC60) but rises to 1630 kg/m3 (SFR60).

extraction.extraction_notes: 21 records = 7 compositions (NE, SFC20/40/60, SFR20/40/60) x 3 impact energies (39.62, 79.02, 118.82 J), all from Table 2. UNITS: the paper reports absorbed energy in joules and SEA in Jm3/kg (an unusual unit; SEA numerically equals absorbed energy / density in kg/m3). Neither maps onto the schema field energy_absorption_mj_m3 (MJ/m3), and the specimen thickness is not given, so no volumetric energy density can be computed. energy_absorption_mj_m3 is therefore left null and the joule values are recorded verbatim in test.specimen_notes and structure.microstructure_notes. Consequently no numeric Properties field is filled for any record - this paper reports no modulus, strength or strain data. Densities converted from kg/m3 to g/cm3 (divide by 1000). Volume fractions converted from percent to fractions. Cure/test temperature set to 25 C because the paper only states 'room temperature'. PARTICLE TYPE: only the SFC series contains hollow particles (fly-ash cenospheres). The SFR series uses solid rubber crumb, which is not a hollow-particle filler, so particle_type is set to 'other' for SFR and for neat epoxy (NE has no filler; particle_volume_fraction = 0). SFR rows are kept because the paper presents them as syntactic foams and they are the direct comparison set. DATA CONFLICT: Table 3 (CoR/ELP) mislabels rows - its 'SFR20' block carries Table 2's SFR40 numbers (3.56/7.08/13.98 J) and its 'SFR40' block duplicates SFC60's numbers (3.31/10.73/11.54 J). Table 2 is internally consistent and is corroborated by the running text (SFR20 = 9.45 J at 118.82 J, Sec. 3.4), so all values were taken from Table 2. Coefficient of restitution and energy-loss percentage have no schema field and were not extracted. Gradation-test layer weights (Figures 7a/7b) are only shown in figures and are not reported numerically per layer, so no per-layer records were created.

extraction.paper_summary: MS thesis (University of Oklahoma, 2025) on Direct Ink Writing (DIW) 3D printing of epoxy syntactic foams. EPON 815C / Epikure 3230 epoxy was filled with 3M hollow glass microballoons (S60, iM16K, iM30K) at 40 wt% relative to epoxy weight, with 1 wt% fumed silica and a thixotropic additive paste to give shear-thinning, yield-stress inks; specimens were printed with a 410 um nozzle at 10 mm/s and cured 2 h at 80 C plus 3 h at 125 C. Cast and printed tensile (0/45/90 deg) and compression (uni- and bi-directional, X/Y) specimens were tested at 1 mm/min: printed parts were more consistent than cast ones, iM30K gave the best tensile properties, S60 the highest compressive modulus, and hybrid iM30K:iM16K inks (1:3, 2:2, 3:1) were used to optimise specific properties, with iM30K_2 iM16K_2 best overall (highest specific strength/modulus, MCF 1551 N, PCF 2103 N). The optimum hybrid ink was printed into 30% infill hexagonal honeycomb cores whose in-plane compression showed higher peak strength in the Y-direction (9.423 MPa) and higher modulus in the X-direction (0.236 GPa).

extraction.extraction_notes:
MS thesis; the whole document (84 pages) was read, including Tables 1-3 and the reference list. Most quantitative results live in figures (Figs. 9, 11-13, 15-17, 19-24, 27) whose individual bar values are not tabulated, so only values stated explicitly in the running text or in the three tables were extracted; everything else was left null rather than read off plots.

Unit conversions: tensile/compressive moduli GPa -> MPa (x1000). Specific properties converted from GPa/(kg/m3) or MPa/(kg/m3) to the schema's MPa per g/cm3 by multiplying by 1e6 or 1e3 respectively: cast iM30K specific tensile modulus 8.88e-4 GPa/(kg/m3) -> 888 MPa/(g/cc) and specific tensile strength 4.42e-2 MPa/(kg/m3) -> 44.2 MPa/(g/cc); hybrid 2:2 compressive specific strength 0.081 MPa/(kg/m3) -> 81 MPa/(g/cc) and specific modulus 4.24e-4 GPa/(kg/m3) -> 424 MPa/(g/cc); honeycomb X 0.00051 GPa/(kg/m3) -> 510 and 0.0130 MPa/(kg/m3) -> 13.0; honeycomb Y 0.00042 -> 420 and 0.0232 -> 23.2 (Sec. 4.4 restates these as 0.00052 and 0.00041; the Sec. 4.3 values were used). Energy absorption for the 1:3 hybrid was converted from the reported SEA of 41.393 J/g using the paper's own measured density of 0.635 g/cm3, giving 26.28 MJ/m3; the raw EA (4.360 J) and MCF/PCF forces have no schema field and are recorded in specimen_notes.

Particle wall_thickness_ratio (eta = inner/outer radius) was computed from Table 1 mean diameter and wall thickness: S60 (15-1.49)/15 = 0.901, iM16K (10-0.72)/10 = 0.928, iM30K (7.65-0.70)/7.65 = 0.908. Particle loading is reported only as '40 wt% relative to the weight of epoxy', i.e. 40 parts per 100 parts resin, not a weight fraction of the whole composite, so particle_weight_fraction was left null and the loading recorded in additional_fillers; no particle volume fractions are given anywhere in the thesis (only qualitative statements that iM16K gives the highest and iM30K the lowest volume fraction at fixed weight fraction).

Caveats: (1) Table 3 (area-corrected strengths, 42.33/38.00/40.23 MPa as-measured and 73.23/68.78/96.55 MPa corrected for 0/45/90 deg) does not state which base ink the 'example specimen' came from; it appears in the base-ink section immediately after the iM30K SEM discussion, so iM30K was assumed - confidence lowered to 0.5 for those three records. (2) The hybrid tensile strengths 42.45 and 37.70 MPa are stated in the same sentence that names the 90 deg orientation only for the 43.05 MPa value; the 90 deg attribution for the other two is inferred (confidence 0.6). (3) The specific compressive modulus 0.000424 GPa/(kg/m3) is the top of a stated range and was attributed to the 2:2 hybrid on the basis of the Chapter 5 statement that it had the highest specific modulus. (4) The reported 2:2 compressive specific strength (0.081 MPa/(kg/m3) x 0.735 g/cm3 implies ~59 MPa) sits above the text's statement that printed peak compressive strengths 'remained below 50 MPa' for the base inks; both are reported as-is. (5) Base-ink compression results are given mostly as ranges (modulus 0.236-0.590 GPa for iM16K/iM30K, peak strength 28.68-49.21 MPa across all inks, strain at peak 0.104-0.245 mm/mm) without per-configuration attribution, so only the S60 Bi-X modulus of 0.619 GPa could be recorded; the S60 minimum strain at peak of 0.104 and the iM16K/iM30K maximum of 0.245 are noted here but not assigned to records. (6) Cast compression is described only as 'certain cast specimens reached compressive strengths exceeding 60 MPa' - no record created. (7) Rheology results (Herschel-Bulkley tau0 = 67.56 / 93.32 / 200.00 Pa and wall shear stress 497.87 / 448.11 / 853.23 Pa for S60 / iM16K / iM30K in Table 2; amplitude-sweep dynamic yield stresses 75.016 / 71.561 / 43.420 Pa) have no schema field and are not recorded as properties. (8) Test temperature is not stated; 25 C was used because all printing and testing was done under ambient laboratory conditions. Crosshead rate was 1 mm/min for all tests but specimen gauge lengths/heights are not given, so no strain rate could be computed. (9) Cure was 2 h at 80 C then 3 h at 125 C; 125 C recorded as the process temperature. (10) The honeycomb records describe an architected 30% infill structure, not a bulk foam, so their moduli/strengths are structural rather than material properties.

extraction.paper_summary: Archaeological conservation science paper (Int. J. Conservation Science 17(1), 2026) on a Late Period polychrome wooden coffin excavated at Rass Algesr, Saqqara, Egypt. OM, SEM-EDX, Raman and FTIR identified the pigments (yellow ochre/goethite and orpiment, Egyptian blue/cuprorivaite, hematite red, calcite white, carbon black), a calcium carbonate ground layer, a linen fabric layer and animal glue binder. Conservation comprised mechanical and chemical cleaning, consolidation with Klucel G, reattachment of the gesso with 10% Primal AC33, and filling the gesso edges with glass microballoons in 15% w/v Paraloid B72 in acetone.
extraction.extraction_notes: Off-topic for syntactic foam Process-Structure-Property extraction. The only hollow-particle content is a conservation filler: 'Using a spatula, glass microballoons containing Paraloid B72 in 15% w/v acetone were applied. The microballoons were then coated with earth pigments.' (Sec. 'Filling the edges of the ground layer', p. 54, repeated in the Conclusion). This is a gap-filling putty applied by hand to an artefact, not a characterized hollow-particle composite: no particle grade, size, density, volume or weight fraction, no foam density, and no mechanical, thermal or any other property measurement of the microballoon/Paraloid mixture is reported anywhere in the paper. The paper's only quantitative material data concern pigment chemistry (EDX elements, Raman/FTIR band positions), painted-layer thickness (100 micron), and consolidant concentrations (Klucel G 0.5% and 1% in ethyl alcohol, Primal AC33 10%, Paraloid B72 15% w/v, ethanol:water 1:1). This paper was almost certainly retrieved by the keyword 'glass microballoons'. is_syntactic_foam_paper set to false and no records emitted.

extraction.paper_summary: An art-conservation case study on the deterioration and restoration of scagliola (imitation-marble decorative plaster) in Zafaran Palace, Cairo. Historic scagliola samples were characterised by digital microscopy, SEM-EDX and XRD, showing a calcite (CaCO3) dominated, heterogeneous material with cavities, microcracks and exfoliation. The authors propose a new loss-completion putty made of hollow glass microballoons mixed with Paraloid B-72 dissolved in toluene (20%) plus colour oxides and zinc, and judge it successful by visual comparison and SEM-EDX/XRD of the cured filler; no mechanical or physical property measurements of the microballoon composite are reported.
extraction.extraction_notes: Flagged off-topic for the syntactic-foam Process-Structure-Property dataset. The paper is a conservation-science case study of historical scagliola, not a materials study of hollow-particle composites. It does describe a microballoon-filled polymer putty (hollow glass microballoons in Paraloid B-72 / toluene at 20% concentration, with colour oxides and zinc, applied by spatula and cured >3 months, then sanded), which is technically a syntactic filler, but the paper reports no quantitative composite property whatsoever: no composite density, porosity, modulus, strength, particle volume or weight fraction, and no mechanical testing of any kind. The only numbers given are (a) supplier data for the microballoons themselves - bulk density 140-150 g/l, specific density 0.20 g/cm3, particle size 50 um with sizing up to 200 um; (b) EDX elemental weight/atomic percentages for the historic scagliola (Table 2: e.g. O 50.85, Ca 34.60, Si 4.27, C 5.05 wt%) and for the completion material (Table 4: Ca 70.55, O 16.06, C 6.00, Si 5.82, Al 1.04 wt%); and (c) qualitative SEM observations that the completed material has more compact grains and fewer cavities than the original. None of these are Process-Structure-Property records under the schema, so records is empty. The whole file (14 pages, through the reference list) was read; there are no property tables elsewhere in the paper.

extraction.paper_summary: Aluminium matrix syntactic foams were made by stir casting Al-2014 alloy with 15, 20 and 25 vol% untreated fly ash cenospheres (60-90 um) and tested for dry sliding wear on a pin-on-disc tribometer (ASTM G99) at 5-25 N load and 4-8 m/s sliding velocity over 2000 m. Increasing cenosphere content lowered the specific wear rate and the friction coefficient (0.46-0.57 across the 15 runs), with the lowest wear at 25 vol%. A Gaussian Process Regression surrogate (training R2 = 0.9228, hold-out R2 = 0.8221) plus Sobol global sensitivity analysis showed cenosphere content (S1 = 0.4963) and applied load (S1 = 0.4752) dominate wear, while sliding velocity is almost irrelevant (S1 = 0.0257).

extraction.extraction_notes: This is a genuine hollow-particle (cenosphere) metal-matrix syntactic foam paper, but it reports ONLY tribological responses - friction coefficient, weight loss, wear rate and specific wear rate. None of these map to any field in the Properties schema, so every property field is null and the measured tribological numbers are recorded verbatim in test.specimen_notes for each of the 15 I-optimal design runs of Table 1. test_type is set to 'other' (dry sliding pin-on-disc); strain_rate_per_s is left null because sliding velocity (m/s) is not a strain rate. No mechanical properties (modulus, strength, density) and no measured foam density are reported anywhere in the paper. Cenosphere bulk density is given only as a range (0.6-0.9 g/cm3) and particle size only as a sieve range (60-90 um), so particle_true_density_g_cc and particle_mean_diameter_um are left null. Melt temperature is given as a range (750-800 C) so cure_or_process_temperature_c is left null. matrix_porosity_fraction uses the ImageJ-measured localized micro-porosity area fractions stated in Sec. 3.1 (<2.8% area for 20% FAC, 3.6% for 25% FAC); the paper states quantitative porosity measurement was not performed for the 15% composition, so it is null there. The 15%/20%/25% cenosphere contents are explicitly by volume, entered as fractions 0.15/0.20/0.25. Table 1 rows appear in the extracted text as one value per line; evidence quotes reproduce each row's values in column order. Values cited from other authors (Mehta et al., Zhang et al., Hussein and Eqal, Rugele et al., Doddamani et al.) in the Introduction/Discussion are literature comparisons for other material systems and were not extracted as records. GPR/Sobol results are model outputs about wear, not material properties, so they are summarised only.

extraction.paper_summary: Ukrainian-language master's thesis (National University of Shipbuilding, Mykolaiv, 2023) on the finite-element stress-strain analysis of buoyancy blocks made of syntactic foam (spheroplastic) containing hollow technical-porcelain ceramic macrospheres, for deep-sea vehicles. Chapters 1-2 review buoyancy materials, ceramic hollow-sphere fillers, packing schemes (volume filling coefficients 0.523 cubic to 0.741 hexagonal) and manufacturing routes (casting vs vacuum injection). Chapters 3-4 use ANSYS Student to compute principal stresses in a 100 mm diameter porcelain shell (wall thickness varied 0.25-1.5 mm) embedded with bonded (adhesive) contact in a 300x300 mm syntactic-foam cube under 1 MPa external hydrostatic pressure (equivalent to 100 m depth), varying the distance from the free surface (0.1-40 mm) and the gap between two neighbouring shells (0.2-80 mm). Conclusions: stress concentrations in the foam reach ~30 units near the surface and up to ~3.5 units between close spheres; shells must be buried at least ~15 mm from the surface and spaced at least ~15 mm apart, so bonded (adhesive) contact between ceramic macrospheres and syntactic foam is judged irrational compared with leaving a water-connected gap.

extraction.extraction_notes: Ukrainian master's thesis; 'сферопластик' (spheroplastic) is the Ukrainian term for syntactic foam, so the paper is on-topic (hollow-particle composite), but it is a finite-element modelling study rather than an experimental one and contains very little tabulated quantitative property data. Only two tables carry material properties: Table 1.1 (general ranges) and Table 3.1 (single values used as FEM inputs). Record 1 uses Table 3.1 (density 600 kg/m3 -> 0.6 g/cm3, compressive strength 60 MPa, modulus 7 GPa -> 7000 MPa) because those are unambiguous single numbers; the Table 1.1 ranges (600-800 kg/m3, 60-80 MPa, 6-8 GPa) and the 700 kg/m3 density quoted on the assignment sheet are recorded in microstructure_notes rather than as invented midpoints. These constants were neither measured nor computed by the author and no source is cited, so data_origin is 'secondary' with the absence of a citation flagged here. Porcelain shell constants (2500 kg/m3, 410 MPa compressive strength, 60 GPa modulus in Table 3.1; 2400 kg/m3, 400-600 MPa, 60-70 GPa in Table 1.1) are constituent, not composite, values and so are kept in text fields, not as records. Record 2 documents the modelled composite; note that the filler is a 100 mm macrosphere, so particle_mean_diameter_um = 100000 um is correct but is orders of magnitude larger than the usual microballoon and should not be mixed with microsphere data. All FEM outputs (minimum and maximum principal stress in the shell, minimum principal stress and stress intensity in the foam, versus shell thickness, distance to surface and inter-sphere gap) are shown only as figures (Figs. 3.9-3.20, 4.3-4.10); the loading is a unit pressure so the results are dimensionless concentration factors, and no numeric stress value is stated in text or a table apart from the summary statements 'up to 30 units' near the free surface, '1.6 to 4.5 for thin shells and 1 to 1.8 for thick-walled shells' between contacting spheres, '3.5 units worst / 0.8 units best' between spheres, and a loss of load-bearing capacity of about 5x when shells touch. Those are concentration factors with no schema field, so they are kept in evidence/notes and no property value was read off a plot. Other numbers in the review chapter that were not turned into records because they are quoted from other works or are generic: water absorption 0.74-0.75% for epoxy/glass-sphere composites (ref [10]), specific buoyancy of spheroplastics 3300-4500 N/m3, typical microsphere diameters 50-200 um, packing volume-filling coefficients 0.523-0.741 (Table 2.1, ref [3]), depth limits for various shell materials (titanium 3000 m, thermoplastics 1000 m, GRP 4000 m, ceramics up to 5000-11000 m), and a rule that spheroplastic collapse pressure is set 1.5x above the service depth pressure.
